Lower-limb arterial Doppler (duplex) ultrasound is the first-line non-invasive test for peripheral arterial disease (PAD). It combines B-mode imaging of the vessel wall, colour Doppler to spot turbulence, and spectral (pulsed-wave) Doppler to read the waveform and measure velocities — letting you localise a stenosis, grade its severity, and map disease before angioplasty or bypass.

1Know the normal waveform: TRIPHASIC
A healthy peripheral (high-resistance) limb artery gives a triphasic spectral trace: a sharp systolic upstroke (forward flow), a brief early-diastolic flow reversal below the baseline (elastic recoil against high peripheral resistance), then a small late-diastolic forward flow. The crisp reversal component is the hallmark of a healthy, compliant, unobstructed vessel.
2Waveform degradation with proximal disease
Distal to a significant stenosis or occlusion the waveform progressively damps: TRIPHASIC → BIPHASIC (reversal component lost) → MONOPHASIC (low-velocity, rounded, continuous forward flow with slow systolic upstroke). A monophasic, damped signal downstream tells you significant disease sits proximal to your probe.
Monophasic damped waveform at ankle→significant stenosis/occlusion proximally — trace up the leg to find the level
3Localise and grade with velocities
At a stenosis, flow accelerates. Compare the peak systolic velocity (PSV) within the narrowed segment to the PSV in the normal segment just proximal — the velocity ratio. A ratio >2:1 indicates a haemodynamically significant ≥50% stenosis; the higher the ratio and PSV, the tighter the lesion. An occluded segment shows no colour or spectral flow, with collaterals reconstituting vessels distally.
Velocity ratio >2:1 across a segment ≈ ≥50% diameter stenosis.
Absent colour + absent spectral signal = occlusion.
Post-stenotic turbulence (spectral broadening) marks the lesion site.
4ABPI — the bedside adjunct
The ankle-brachial pressure index is highest ankle systolic pressure ÷ highest brachial systolic pressure, measured with a hand-held Doppler probe. It quantifies perfusion and complements the duplex map.
✔0.9–1.3
Normal perfusion.
⚠0.5–0.9
Intermittent claudication.
✖<0.5
Critical limb ischaemia.
↑>1.3
Falsely elevated — incompressible calcified vessels (diabetes, CKD).
5From map to management
Duplex maps the level, length and severity of disease to plan intervention: short focal stenoses suit angioplasty ± stenting, whereas long occlusions or multilevel disease favour surgical bypass (duplex also assesses vein conduit). Where duplex is inconclusive or a full arterial roadmap is needed, CT or MR angiography are the cross-sectional alternatives. First-line management of stable claudication remains conservative: supervised exercise, smoking cessation, statin and antiplatelet, and BP/diabetes control.
🚩 Acute limb ischaemia is a surgical emergency — the 6 Ps: Pain, Pallor, Pulselessness, Paraesthesia, Perishingly cold, Paralysis. It threatens limb viability within hours (embolus or acute thrombosis) and needs urgent revascularisation or embolectomy. Do not delay for elaborate imaging — an immediate vascular surgical opinion and systemic heparinisation come first. Fixed mottling, paralysis and sensory loss suggest an unsalvageable limb.
🎓 Let the waveform tell you where to look: a damped monophasic signal at the ankle means the problem is upstream, so walk the probe proximally until the trace becomes triphasic again — the transition point brackets the culprit lesion. And always sanity-check a reassuringly "normal" ABPI in a diabetic against the waveforms: an incompressible calcified vessel can give a falsely high index masking severe disease.

Renal artery Doppler is the non-invasive first-line screen for renal artery stenosis (RAS) — it combines grey-scale assessment of kidney size with colour and spectral Doppler of the main renal arteries and the intrarenal vessels, looking for a jet of high velocity at the narrowing and a dampened waveform downstream.
1Why order it — the clinical triggers
RAS causes secondary hypertension via renin-angiotensin activation. Suspect it and request Doppler when the blood pressure or kidney behaves oddly. Key indications: resistant/refractory hypertension (uncontrolled on ≥3 drugs including a diuretic); hypertension in a young person, especially a woman (fibromuscular dysplasia); an epigastric or flank bruit; "flash" pulmonary oedema (recurrent sudden pulmonary oedema without a cardiac cause); unexplained or asymmetric renal size; and a rise in creatinine after starting an ACE inhibitor or ARB — a classic clue to bilateral RAS, or RAS to a solitary kidney.
2The two causes — different patients, different segments
Cause shapes both the patient and the lesion location.
🫀Atherosclerosis
Older patients, cardiovascular risk factors. Lesion is ostial/proximal (at the aortic origin). Commonest overall cause of RAS.
🧬Fibromuscular dysplasia
Younger women. Lesion is mid-to-distal vessel, classic "string of beads" on angiography. Responds well to angioplasty.
3Reading the Doppler — direct and indirect signs
Significant stenosis produces a high-velocity jet at the narrowing and a dampened waveform beyond it.
Narrowed lumen accelerates flow→raised peak systolic velocity + downstream tardus-parvus
Raised peak systolic velocity (PSV) at the stenosis, e.g. >180–200 cm/s — the direct sign.
Elevated renal-aortic ratio (RAR >3.5) — renal artery PSV divided by aortic PSV, correcting for cardiac output.
Downstream intrarenal "tardus-parvus" waveform: delayed, slow systolic upstroke (prolonged acceleration time) and a low, rounded peak.
Low resistive index distally; also note kidney size — an atrophic kidney (<8–9 cm) suggests long-standing disease.
4Confirming and managing
Doppler is the screen; anatomical confirmation is by CT angiography or MR angiography. Management is often medical: an ACEi/ARB with careful renal-function and potassium monitoring, plus cardiovascular risk reduction (statin, antiplatelet, smoking cessation, BP control). Angioplasty ± stent is used selectively — for FMD, recurrent flash pulmonary oedema, or rapidly declining renal function. Importantly, routine stenting of atherosclerotic RAS does not clearly improve outcomes over optimal medical therapy in randomised trials.
🚩 Bilateral RAS (or RAS to a solitary functioning kidney) with a sharp creatinine rise after starting an ACEi/ARB: efferent arteriolar tone was maintaining glomerular filtration pressure. Stop the drug and seek urgent renal/vascular input.
🎓 A young woman with hypertension and an abdominal bruit points to fibromuscular dysplasia ("string of beads", mid-vessel, angioplasty-responsive); an older arteriopath with an ostial lesion points to atherosclerosis (medical therapy, stenting rarely helps). On Doppler: think high velocity at the stenosis, slow waveform beyond it.

The liver has a dual blood supply — the portal vein (~75%) and hepatic artery (~25%) bring blood IN, and the hepatic veins drain it OUT into the IVC. Portal and hepatic vein Doppler ultrasound interrogates all three, making it the front-line, non-invasive test for portal hypertension and vascular liver disease.

1The normal portal vein
Normal portal vein flow is hepatopetal (towards the liver — displayed above the baseline by convention), gently phasic with respiration/cardiac cycle, and low velocity (typically 15–40 cm/s). The main portal vein measures up to ~13 mm at rest. The waveform is a soft undulating band, quite unlike the sharp pulsatility of the adjacent hepatic artery.
2Portal hypertension
Usually a consequence of cirrhosis. As sinusoidal resistance rises, portal flow slows, loses its phasicity, and may ultimately reverse.
Portal flow becomes slow, monophasic, then reversed (hepatofugal)→rising portal pressure with decompression through collaterals
Dilated portal vein >13 mm
Splenomegaly & ascites
Recanalised umbilical vein (paraumbilical)
Porto-systemic collaterals / varices (gastro-oesophageal, splenorenal)
The single most specific Doppler sign is hepatofugal (reversed) portal flow — blood fleeing the high-pressure liver.
3The vascular emergencies
Two occlusive syndromes must be recognised on Doppler:
🩸Portal vein thrombosis
Echogenic thrombus filling the portal vein lumen with absent flow on Doppler. Bland thrombus is avascular; tumour thrombus shows arterial flow WITHIN the clot — a red flag for underlying HCC. Chronic occlusion produces cavernous transformation (a tangle of collateral vessels replacing the vein).
🚱Budd-Chiari syndrome
Hepatic vein outflow obstruction. Look for absent / reversed / turbulent hepatic vein flow, hepatic vein thrombosis or webs, caudate lobe hypertrophy (its separate IVC drainage is spared) and ascites.
4Shunts & transplant surveillance
TIPS (transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunt) surveillance uses Doppler velocities to detect shunt stenosis — an abnormal velocity (too high at a stenosis, or too low with a change over time) flags dysfunction. After liver transplant, Doppler confirms patency of the hepatic artery, portal vein and hepatic veins; hepatic artery thrombosis is the feared early complication, threatening the graft's biliary tree (which depends solely on arterial supply).
🚩 Acute portal vein thrombosis or Budd-Chiari presenting with abdominal pain, tense ascites and deranged LFTs needs urgent hepatology input and consideration of anticoagulation. Arterial flow within a portal vein thrombus (tumour thrombus) strongly implies hepatocellular carcinoma — escalate for staging.
🎓 Direction is diagnosis: normal portal flow runs towards the liver (hepatopetal). Slow, monophasic, or reversed (hepatofugal) flow = portal hypertension; absent flow with echogenic lumen = thrombosis; blocked outflow with caudate hypertrophy = Budd-Chiari.

The arteriovenous fistula (AVF) is the lifeline of a haemodialysis patient, and ultrasound is the imaging workhorse at both ends of its life: before it exists (pre-operative vein mapping to pick the best site) and after it is made (surveillance for maturation and complications). Duplex combines B-mode anatomy with Doppler flow, letting you measure vessel diameters, confirm patency, and quantify access volume flow — the single most important functional number for a fistula.

1Role one: pre-operative vein mapping

Before creating access you assess inflow and outflow. On the arterial side, scan the radial and brachial arteries for diameter, patency and calcification; a heavily calcified or small radial artery predicts failure. Physiologically, the modified Allen's test / palmar arch patency confirms the hand will tolerate loss of radial inflow. On the venous side, measure the cephalic and basilic veins under a light tourniquet — you want a vein that is patent, distensible on augmentation, superficial (not too deep to needle) and ideally ≥2–2.5 mm in diameter.

Good target vein on mapping→patent, distensible, ≥2–2.5 mm, superficial — suitable for AVF

Site selection follows a distal-to-proximal, autologous-first hierarchy. Access preference: AVF > AV graft > central venous catheter. Fistula preference:

1st — radiocephalic ('Brescia–Cimino'): wrist, preserves proximal vessels, lower steal risk.
2nd — brachiocephalic: antecubital, higher flow, easier to needle.
3rd — brachiobasilic transposition: deep basilic vein superficialised in a second stage.
2Role two: surveillance — maturation and access flow

A new fistula must mature before it can be cannulated: the vein must arterialise, dilate and thicken. Ultrasound confirms this using the clinically useful rule of 6s: by about 6 weeks, access flow >600 mL/min, vein diameter >6 mm, and vein depth <6 mm from the skin. Doppler measures the access volume flow rate (cross-sectional area × time-averaged velocity) in the feeding artery or fistula body — a falling flow is the earliest quantitative warning of a failing access.

Flow >600, diameter >6 mm, depth <6 mm at ~6 weeks→mature fistula, ready to cannulate
3Complications to hunt on duplex
📉Stenosis
Commonly juxta-anastomotic or outflow. Raised peak systolic velocity, PSV ratio >2–3 across the lesion, reduced access flow — causes poor maturation and threatens thrombosis.
🩸Thrombosis
No Doppler flow, echogenic clot filling the lumen, absent thrill/bruit clinically. An access emergency.
🎈Aneurysm / pseudoaneurysm
True aneurysm (all layers) or pseudoaneurysm at repeated puncture sites — yin-yang flow on colour Doppler; risk of rupture and skin breakdown.
🥶Steal syndrome
Fistula diverts arterial flow from the hand — distal pain, pallor, cold, weak pulse. Doppler shows retrograde arterial flow distal to the anastomosis.
💓High-output access
Very high access flow (often >1.5–2 L/min) can precipitate or worsen high-output cardiac failure — flag on volume-flow measurement.
🚩 A thrombosed access — absent thrill and bruit with no Doppler flow — is an access emergency: refer urgently for thrombectomy / salvage to preserve the dialysis lifeline before the vein is lost. Likewise, steal syndrome with a threatened, ischaemic hand (rest pain, pallor, sensorimotor loss) needs urgent vascular review — the limb takes priority over the fistula.
🎓 Two roles, one probe: map before, watch after. Learn the two numeric rules that examiners love — a good target vein is ≥2–2.5 mm on pre-op mapping, and a mature fistula obeys the rule of 6s (flow >600 mL/min, diameter >6 mm, depth <6 mm by ~6 weeks). Falling access flow and a PSV ratio >2–3 point to the stenosis that is quietly strangling the access.

ULTRASOUND__Echocardiography — Core:
Transthoracic echocardiography (TTE) is the first-line, non-invasive cardiac ultrasound: a probe on the chest wall images the heart in real time to assess chamber size, ventricular function, all four valves, the pericardium and great vessels — no radiation, portable and repeatable at the bedside.

1Where the probe sits — the standard acoustic windows

Bone and air block ultrasound, so the operator moves the probe between windows where the heart abuts the chest wall or upper abdomen. The core windows are:

Parasternal — long-axis and short-axis views: LV, aortic and mitral valves, wall thickness.
Apical — 4-chamber, 5-chamber, 2-chamber and 3-chamber views: all four chambers, EF, mitral/tricuspid inflow.
Subcostal — from below the xiphisternum: excellent for pericardial effusion and the IVC.
Suprasternal — from the notch: aortic arch and great vessels.
2The imaging modalities and what each one answers
🖥️2D imaging
Real-time anatomy: chamber size, wall thickness, wall motion, valve morphology.
📏M-mode
Single-line, high temporal resolution: precise timing and linear measurements.
🌈Colour Doppler
Maps flow direction over anatomy: regurgitant jets and intracardiac shunts.
📈Spectral Doppler
Pulsed and continuous-wave: velocities, pressure gradients and valve areas.
High-velocity jet across a narrowed valve on CW Doppler→apply the modified Bernoulli equation (ΔP = 4v²) to estimate the pressure gradient.
3What a full study reports

A standard TTE systematically works through:

LV systolic function — ejection fraction; regional wall motion abnormalities suggest ischaemia or prior MI.
Diastolic function, chamber dimensions and hypertrophy (e.g. LVH).
All four valves — stenosis and regurgitation, graded by Doppler.
Pericardium — effusion and signs of tamponade physiology.
Pulmonary artery pressure — estimated from the tricuspid regurgitation jet velocity.
IVC calibre and collapsibility — estimates right atrial pressure and volume status.
Gross congenital lesions — septal defects, bicuspid aortic valve.
4Indications, strengths and limits

Indications: heart failure or breathlessness, murmurs and suspected valve disease, post-MI assessment, cardiomyopathy, endocarditis screening, pre-operative risk assessment, and palpitations or arrhythmia work-up.

Advantages: non-invasive, no ionising radiation, portable to the bedside and easily repeated. Limitations: operator-dependent, with poor acoustic windows in obesity, COPD (hyperinflated lungs) and ventilated patients — situations where transoesophageal echo (TOE), passing the probe down the oesophagus behind the heart, gives superior images.

🚩 A breathless, hypotensive patient with a large pericardial effusion and diastolic collapse of the right atrium and right ventricle on echo is in cardiac tamponade — a peri-arrest emergency requiring urgent echo-guided pericardiocentesis. Separately, a newly reduced ejection fraction in a patient with chest pain warrants urgent cardiology referral.
🎓 TTE is the workhorse first-line cardiac imaging test: think of it as answering four questions in every study — how well is the LV pumping (EF and wall motion), are the valves working, is there fluid around the heart, and what are the filling pressures (IVC and TR jet). Remember its blind spot: image quality is only as good as the acoustic window, so reach for TOE when the chest wall gets in the way.

Transoesophageal echocardiography (TOE, or TEE) passes an ultrasound probe down the oesophagus so the transducer sits directly behind the left atrium. With no lung or chest wall in the way, it gives markedly superior resolution of posterior structures — the left atrium, left atrial appendage, mitral valve, prosthetic valves, aorta and interatrial septum — than a standard transthoracic scan (TTE).

1Why the oesophageal window wins

The oesophagus lies immediately posterior to the heart, so a probe placed there is closer to posterior structures and free of the acoustic barriers (rib, lung, subcutaneous fat) that degrade TTE. Higher-frequency imaging then becomes possible, giving finer spatial resolution of small, mobile or deep targets.

Posterior structure that TTE images poorly→TOE is the test of choice
Left atrial appendage — essentially invisible on TTE, seen clearly on TOE.
Prosthetic valves — metallic shadowing from the front on TTE is bypassed from behind.
Interatrial septum and thoracic aorta — well profiled for shunts and dissection.
2Key indications

TOE is requested when TTE is non-diagnostic or when the anatomy demands its resolution.

🦠Infective endocarditis
Far more sensitive than TTE for vegetations, valve abscess and prosthetic-valve involvement.
🩸Embolic source / pre-cardioversion
Detects LA appendage thrombus in AF before cardioversion or appendage occlusion — TTE cannot see the appendage.
💟Mitral valve mapping
Detailed leaflet and annular assessment before mitral repair; also prosthetic valve dysfunction.
🚑Aortic dissection
Especially in the unstable or intra-operative patient who cannot reach CT.
🫧PFO / ASD & shunts
Interatrial septum imaged with an agitated-saline bubble study to confirm intracardiac shunt.
🔧Intra-operative monitoring
Real-time guidance of valve surgery and haemodynamics during cardiac theatre cases.
3A semi-invasive test — consent, prep and risk

Unlike TTE, TOE is semi-invasive. It needs written consent, a period of fasting, throat local anaesthetic plus sedation, and monitoring during and after the procedure. Small but real risks include oesophageal perforation and aspiration.

Oesophageal stricture, varices, recent oesophageal surgery or unstable c-spine→Contraindicated — do not intubate the oesophagus blindly
🚩 A common exam trap: TOE is used to exclude LA appendage thrombus before cardioversion in AF and to diagnose endocarditis or dissection in unstable patients — but never force the probe against a contraindicated oesophagus. A suspected type A aortic dissection is a surgical emergency, not merely an imaging exercise.
🎓 Remember TOE by what sits behind the oesophagus: the left atrium and its appendage. Whenever a question hinges on the appendage, posterior mitral detail, a prosthetic valve, vegetations, the interatrial septum or the aorta, TOE beats TTE — at the cost of being semi-invasive and needing sedation and consent.

Stress echocardiography combines echo imaging before and during cardiac stress to unmask inducible myocardial ischaemia — and also to assess myocardial viability and selected valve lesions. The core idea: a myocardial segment supplied by a significantly stenosed coronary artery contracts normally at rest but develops a new or worsening regional wall motion abnormality when the heart is stressed. Where the wall goes off tells you which coronary is the culprit.

1How you stress the heart
Stress is delivered in one of two ways. Exercise — treadmill or supine bicycle — is preferred when the patient can exercise, because it adds functional/symptom information. When they can't, use a pharmacological agent: dobutamine increases contractility and heart rate to raise myocardial oxygen demand and provoke ischaemia (a graded, incremental infusion, sometimes topped up with atropine to reach target heart rate), or a vasodilator (e.g. dipyridamole/adenosine) to create coronary steal. Images are acquired at rest and at peak stress and compared side by side.
2The principle — inducible ischaemia
A coronary stenosis may allow adequate resting flow but cannot meet demand under stress. The under-perfused segment stops thickening normally: it becomes hypokinetic (reduced) or akinetic (absent). A new or worsening regional wall motion abnormality on stress is a positive test for inducible ischaemia, and the affected territory localises the diseased vessel (e.g. septal/anterior → LAD; inferior → RCA; lateral → circumflex).
Segment normal at rest, becomes hypokinetic/akinetic on stress → inducible ischaemia = positive test; territory names the culprit coronary
Normal response = every segment thickens more with stress and the cavity gets smaller.
Fixed abnormality present at rest that does not change = old infarct/scar, not inducible ischaemia.
3What it's used for
🫀Stable chest pain
A NICE-endorsed non-invasive functional test for patients with an intermediate pre-test probability of coronary artery disease.
💤Viability / hibernation
Low-dose dobutamine shows a biphasic response — contraction improves at low dose then worsens at high dose — marking viable myocardium that may recover after revascularisation.
🩺Low-flow low-gradient AS
Dobutamine distinguishes true severe aortic stenosis from pseudo-severe AS when the gradient is low because the ventricle is weak.

Advantages: no ionising radiation, and it delivers combined functional and anatomical information at the bedside.

4Cautions and contraindications
Avoid or use great care in acute coronary syndrome, severe uncontrolled hypertension, significant arrhythmia, and severe symptomatic aortic stenosis (particularly for exercise stress). Resuscitation facilities must be immediately available because the test deliberately provokes ischaemia.
🚩 If stress provokes chest pain, ST changes, a large new wall-motion abnormality, or hypotension, stop the test, treat the patient, and refer for urgent coronary angiography. This is a strongly positive result signalling significant, flow-limiting coronary disease.
🎓 Rest normal + stress abnormal = inducible ischaemia (culprit stenosis). Rest abnormal + no change = scar. Rest abnormal + biphasic low-dose improvement = viable/hibernating myocardium worth revascularising. Same probe, three very different answers.

Contrast echocardiography uses gas-filled microbubbles as an ultrasound contrast agent to enhance the study. There are two clinically distinct flavours you must not confuse: an agitated saline “bubble study” to hunt for a right-to-left shunt, and commercial microbubble LV opacification to sharpen a technically difficult scan. Bubbles are intensely echogenic because the gas–blood interface reflects almost all the incident ultrasound.

1Agitated saline “bubble study” — the shunt hunt

Sterile saline is mixed vigorously between two syringes via a three-way tap (often with a tiny amount of the patient’s blood or air) to generate a cloud of large bubbles, then injected into a peripheral arm vein while imaging an apical 4-chamber view. In normal physiology the bubbles opacify the right atrium and right ventricle, then are completely filtered by the pulmonary capillary bed and never reach the left heart.

Bubbles in the LEFT heart within ~3–5 beats→intracardiac right-to-left shunt (PFO or ASD)
Bubbles in the LEFT heart after ~5 beats (delayed)→intrapulmonary shunt, e.g. pulmonary AVM

Because a PFO is a flap valve, the shunt may only open when right atrial pressure transiently exceeds left — so the study is repeated during a Valsalva manoeuvre or cough (with release) to unmask it. The headline indication is the work-up of cryptogenic / young stroke, looking for a PFO that could permit paradoxical embolism.

Right heart opacifies first — bubbles follow venous return to the RA/RV.
Count the beats: early = cardiac, late = pulmonary.
Always provoke with Valsalva/cough — a resting-only study can miss a PFO.
2Contrast microbubble LV opacification — the border sharpener

These are commercial encapsulated microbubbles (e.g. shelled with a lipid or albumin membrane) that are small and stable enough to cross the pulmonary capillaries intact and reach the left ventricle. Injected intravenously, they opacify the LV cavity and are used when the endocardial borders are poorly seen on a technically difficult study (obese patient, ventilated, poor windows).

Uses: improving the accuracy of ejection fraction assessment, unmasking an apical thrombus (a filling defect in the opacified apex), diagnosing apical hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (a spade-shaped cavity), and — with dedicated protocols — myocardial perfusion imaging.

Poor endocardial definition / uninterpretable EF→LV opacification contrast to define borders
🔵Agitated saline
Large bubbles, stay in the RIGHT heart unless there is a shunt. Cheap, bedside, no radiation. Detects PFO/ASD & pulmonary AVM.
🔵Commercial microbubbles
Small, cross the lungs to opacify the LV. Define borders for EF, find apical thrombus / apical HCM, perfusion imaging.
🚩 A PFO or ASD with a documented right-to-left shunt in a patient with stroke means possible paradoxical embolism — refer to a cardiology/neurology MDT to consider PFO closure. A large shunt causing hypoxia (classically platypnoea-orthodeoxia — breathlessness and desaturation on sitting/standing, relieved by lying flat) warrants urgent assessment.
🎓 Remember the one-line discriminator: agitated saline stays right unless there’s a shunt; commercial microbubbles go left to show you the LV. “Early bubbles = hole in the heart, late bubbles = leaky lungs.”

Focused cardiac ultrasound (FoCUS, also called FICE or focused echo) is a goal-directed, point-of-care scan performed at the bedside by trained clinicians — not cardiac physiologists — to answer specific binary questions in the acutely unwell or peri-arrest patient. It is qualitative, rapid and always interpreted alongside the clinical picture. Crucially, it is not a substitute for a full transthoracic echo (TTE), which is a comprehensive, quantitative study done by an accredited sonographer.

1What FoCUS actually answers

FoCUS is deliberately narrow. It exists to answer a handful of high-yield, life-or-death questions fast, so management can change within minutes:

  • Pericardial effusion / tamponade? — is fluid compressing the heart?
  • LV function — grossly good or poor? ("eyeball" ejection fraction, not a measured number)
  • RV dilatation/strain — a dilated, strained right ventricle suggests massive pulmonary embolism.
  • Volume status — via the IVC (size and collapsibility) to gauge fluid responsiveness / right atrial pressure.
  • Gross valve or obvious structural abnormality.
Full quantitative EF, valve gradients, diastology needed→refer for a formal TTE — that is not the job of FoCUS
2Standard views

FoCUS uses the same windows as TTE, but reads them qualitatively. Know the four core views and what each is best for:

Subcostal 4-chamber — the workhorse in arrest; probe under the xiphisternum aimed at the left shoulder. Best single view for effusion and gross function; can be obtained without interrupting compressions.
Subcostal IVC — long-axis of the IVC entering the right atrium; assess diameter and inspiratory collapse for volume status.
Parasternal long axis (PLAX) — LV, LA, aortic and mitral valves, and dependent pericardial fluid.
Parasternal short axis (PSAX) — LV in cross-section (radial function), and the "D-shaped" septum of RV pressure/volume overload.
Apical 4-chamber — all four chambers side-by-side; direct RV:LV size comparison and chamber function.
3Role in peri-arrest / cardiac arrest

The headline use of FoCUS is hunting for reversible causes — the 4 Hs and 4 Ts — during the rhythm-check pause of an ALS arrest. The subcostal view is placed ready so the image is captured in the <10-second pulse-check window without delaying chest compressions. It is especially good at flagging:

  • Tamponade — a still heart swinging in a rim of pericardial fluid.
  • Massive PE — a grossly dilated, strained RV (obstructive cause).
  • Hypovolaemia — an empty, vigorously collapsing LV and flat IVC.
  • Tension pneumothorax — with adjunctive lung ultrasound (absent lung sliding).

Beyond arrest, FoCUS underpins structured shock assessments (e.g. RUSH-type protocols), helping distinguish cardiogenic vs hypovolaemic vs obstructive shock at the bedside.

4Reversible causes at a glance
💧Tamponade
Pericardial fluid + compressed chambers → urgent pericardiocentesis.
🫁Massive PE
Dilated, strained RV (RV > LV) → consider thrombolysis.
🩸Hypovolaemia
Small hyperdynamic LV + flat, collapsing IVC → fluids.
⚠️Tension PTX
Lung US: absent sliding/lung point → needle/finger decompression.
🚩 In cardiac arrest or peri-arrest, a pericardial effusion around a still heart, or a grossly dilated right ventricle, flags tamponade or massive PE — act on the reversible cause immediately (pericardiocentesis / thrombolysis). Never let scanning interrupt or prolong pauses in chest compressions; image in the pulse-check window only.
🎓 FoCUS answers binary questions, not precise ones: "is there fluid?", "is the RV big?", "is the LV moving?". Its power in the sick patient is speed and integration with the clinical picture — the moment you need a number, a gradient or a definitive structural diagnosis, that is a formal TTE by an accredited sonographer, not a bedside focused scan.

ULTRASOUND__Echocardiography — Assessmen:
Every echo report answers two separate questions about the left ventricle: how well does it squeeze (systolic function) and how well does it relax and fill (diastolic function)? These two axes underpin the two great phenotypes of heart failure — HFrEF (a weak pump) and HFpEF (a stiff pump) — and a patient can be breathless from either.

1Systolic function — the ejection fraction

Systolic function is contraction and emptying. The headline number is the ejection fraction (EF), the proportion of blood ejected with each beat:

EF = (EDV − ESV) / EDV

Normal EF is ≥50%. The reference method is Simpson's biplane: trace the LV endocardial border at end-diastole and end-systole in both the apical 4-chamber and apical 2-chamber views; the software sums a stack of discs to give volumes and hence EF. An experienced operator may also "eyeball" it. Supporting measures include fractional shortening (M-mode of LV diameters) and assessment of regional wall motion for territories of ischaemia.

EF ≤40% with symptoms/signs→HFrEF (reduced EF); EF 41–49% is HFmrEF (mildly reduced); EF ≥50% is preserved
2Diastolic function — relaxation and filling

When EF is preserved but the patient still has heart failure, the problem is a stiff, poorly relaxing ventricle that generates high filling pressures. Diastolic assessment explains HFpEF, which requires: EF ≥50% plus symptoms/signs, plus raised natriuretic peptides (BNP/NT-proBNP), plus a structural or functional abnormality on echo.

Mitral inflow (pulsed Doppler) — E wave (early passive filling) and A wave (atrial kick); the E/A ratio characterises the filling pattern.
Tissue Doppler e′ (e-prime) — velocity of the mitral annulus in early diastole; a low e′ reflects impaired relaxation.
E/e′ ratio — the key surrogate for LV filling pressure; E/e′ >14 suggests elevated left atrial pressure.
Left atrial volume index — a dilated LA is the "HbA1c" of chronic diastolic dysfunction.
TR jet velocity — estimates pulmonary artery systolic pressure; high values suggest downstream congestion.
3Grades of diastolic dysfunction

Diastolic dysfunction progresses through a recognisable sequence as the ventricle stiffens and filling pressures climb:

1Impaired relaxation
E/A <0.8, low e′; filling pressures still normal. Common with ageing and LVH.
2Pseudonormal
E/A back to 0.8–2 but E/e′ and LA size are raised — rising pressures "mask" the pattern.
3Restrictive filling
E/A >2, high E/e′, severe LA enlargement. Stiff ventricle, high pressures — advanced disease.

Causes of HFpEF: hypertension with LVH, ageing, diabetes, obesity, and restrictive/infiltrative disease (e.g. amyloid).

🚩 Acute decompensated heart failure with pulmonary oedema is a medical emergency and needs urgent treatment regardless of EF. A restrictive filling pattern with severe LA enlargement and high E/e′ signals advanced disease; new severe LV systolic impairment warrants cardiology referral and prompt initiation of guideline-directed medical therapy.
🎓 EF answers "can it squeeze?" and diastology answers "can it fill?" — always read them together. A normal EF never excludes heart failure; in HFpEF the EF is preserved by definition, and it is the E/e′, LA volume and natriuretic peptides that reveal the failing, stiff ventricle.

Echocardiography is the first-line, non-invasive tool for grading valvular disease. It combines 2D/3D imaging (valve morphology, mobility, leaflet number and calcification), colour Doppler (regurgitant jets), and spectral Doppler (velocity → pressure) to answer two questions for every valve: is it too tight (stenosis) or too leaky (regurgitation), and how severe is it?

1The physics: turning velocity into pressure

Continuous-wave (CW) Doppler measures the peak blood velocity through a narrowed valve. The modified Bernoulli equation converts this to a pressure gradient:

ΔP = 4v²  (mmHg, where v is peak velocity in m/s)

So a jet of 4 m/s across the aortic valve gives a peak gradient of 4 × 16 = 64 mmHg. Valve area is derived either by direct tracing (planimetry) or by the continuity equation (flow is conserved, so a smaller area means a higher velocity).

High peak velocity on CW Doppler → high gradient → tighter (more stenotic) valve
2Aortic stenosis (AS)

Causes: calcific/degenerative (commonest, elderly), bicuspid valve (younger patients), and rheumatic (developing world, usually with mitral involvement). Severity thresholds:

Peak velocity >4 m/s = severe
Mean gradient >40 mmHg = severe
Aortic valve area <1.0 cm² (or indexed <0.6 cm²/m²) = severe
Low-flow, low-gradient AS (small valve area but low gradient due to poor LV function) → dobutamine stress echo to distinguish true severe AS from pseudo-severe
3Aortic regurgitation (AR)

Colour Doppler shows the diastolic jet flowing back into the LV. Severity markers:

Wide jet width / vena contracta relative to the LVOT = more severe
Short pressure half-time (rapid aortic-LV pressure equalisation) = severe
Holodiastolic flow reversal in the descending/abdominal aorta = severe

Always assess LV size and function: progressive LV dilatation is a key trigger for surgery even before symptoms.

4Mitral regurgitation (MR)

Distinguish primary (a valve problem: degenerative prolapse, flail leaflet, endocarditis) from secondary/functional (a normal valve tethered by a dilated or dysfunctional LV). Quantify with:

Jet area and vena contracta width
PISA method → EROA (effective regurgitant orifice area) and regurgitant volume
Flail leaflet or ruptured chordae, plus LA and LV dilatation
5Mitral stenosis (MS) and the right side

MS is almost always rheumatic. Look for the classic "hockey-stick" diastolic doming of the thickened anterior leaflet, and measure valve area by planimetry or pressure half-time (severe <1.5 cm²). Assess the left atrium for enlargement, thrombus, and spontaneous echo contrast, and note associated AF.

On the right side, the tricuspid regurgitation (TR) jet velocity estimates the RV/pulmonary artery systolic pressure (4v² + RA pressure). If a prosthetic valve is dysfunctional, a transoesophageal echo (TOE) gives superior views of leaflets, jets and vegetations.

🫀Aortic stenosis
Vel >4 m/s, mean >40 mmHg, area <1.0 cm²
💧Aortic regurg
Vena contracta, short PHT, holodiastolic aortic reversal
🔁Mitral regurg
EROA/PISA, flail leaflet, LA/LV dilatation
🏒Mitral stenosis
Rheumatic, hockey-stick doming, area <1.5 cm²
🚩 Symptomatic severe valve disease is an emergency in the making. Syncope, angina or breathlessness in severe aortic stenosis carries a poor prognosis without valve replacement. Acute severe MR or AR — from infective endocarditis or chordal/papillary rupture — presents with sudden pulmonary oedema and cardiogenic shock and needs urgent cardiology/cardiothoracic referral for intervention (surgery or TAVI).
🎓 Learn the three severe-AS numbers as a set — velocity >4, mean gradient >40, area <1.0 — because the gradient and area can disagree in low-flow states, and that discordance is precisely what triggers a dobutamine stress echo.

A pericardial effusion is fluid between the visceral and parietal pericardium — easy to see on echo, but the number that matters is not the size, it's whether the heart can fill. Tamponade is the moment intrapericardial pressure exceeds chamber filling pressure and the heart is squeezed from the outside. It is a clinical and echo diagnosis, and it kills fast.

1Recognise the effusion

An effusion is an echo-free (anechoic) space between the bright visceral and parietal pericardial layers. If the fluid contains pus, blood, or fibrin strands it becomes complex/echogenic — swirling internal echoes or stranding rather than pure black.

Size is graded by the depth of the echo-free space in diastole: small (<1 cm), moderate (1–2 cm), large (>2 cm). Distribution matters too — circumferential (all around the heart) versus loculated (a walled-off pocket, common post-cardiac-surgery, which can still compress one chamber locally).

2Don't be fooled — the mimics

Two things masquerade as effusion on the parasternal long-axis view:

Fluid tracks anterior to the descending thoracic aorta→pericardial effusion
Fluid tracks posterior to the descending aorta→pleural effusion

The pericardial fat pad is the other trap — it sits anteriorly, often contains fine speckled echoes, and does not extend circumferentially behind the heart. A pure anechoic stripe seen all the way around is fluid, not fat.

3The echo signs of tamponade

Physiology first: as intrapericardial pressure rises, it compresses the lowest-pressure chambers during their lowest-pressure phase. Look for these signs together — no single one is diagnostic.

RA systolic collapse (RA free-wall inversion — occurs when RA pressure is lowest; RV collapse is the diastolic sign) — the earliest and most sensitive sign. The thin-walled atrium buckles first.
RV diastolic collapse — the most specific sign. The RV free wall dips inward in early diastole when RV pressure is lowest.
Plethoric, dilated IVC that fails to collapse >50% with inspiration — reflects a raised right atrial pressure. A near-universal finding; its absence should make you doubt the diagnosis.
Exaggerated respiratory variation in mitral/tricuspid inflow (echocardiographic pulsus paradoxus) — ventricular interdependence causes a septal bounce and a "swinging heart" within the effusion.
4Speed beats size

The pericardium is stiff acutely but stretches over time. This is why how fast fluid accumulates matters more than volume:

⚡Rapid & small = dangerous
Haemopericardium from post-MI free-wall rupture, trauma, aortic dissection, or post-procedure. Even ~150–200 mL can tamponade because the pericardium has no time to stretch.
🐢Slow & large = tolerated
Chronic effusions (malignancy, uraemia, hypothyroidism) can hold 1–2 L with minimal symptoms because the pericardium accommodates gradually.
5Tie it to the bedside & manage

Beck's triad: hypotension, muffled heart sounds, raised JVP. Add tachycardia and pulsus paradoxus (a >10 mmHg inspiratory fall in systolic BP). A breathless, hypotensive patient with these signs and an effusion is tamponade until proven otherwise.

Management: urgent echo-guided pericardiocentesis (or surgical drainage / pericardial window, especially for loculated or post-surgical collections). Support preload with IV fluids while arranging drainage, and avoid over-diuresis — a tamponading heart is preload-dependent and dropping filling pressure can precipitate collapse.

🚩 Tamponade is a peri-arrest emergency. A hypotensive, breathless patient with a pericardial effusion and RA/RV diastolic collapse needs immediate pericardiocentesis — do not wait for a formal cardiology list. In a PEA arrest with an effusion on point-of-care echo, drain it as a reversible cause.
🎓 Size tells you there's fluid; physiology tells you it's tamponade. Chamber collapse plus a plethoric non-collapsing IVC in a shocked patient outranks any measurement — treat the patient, not the millimetres.

Global longitudinal strain (GLS) is an advanced echocardiographic measure of myocardial deformation. Rather than looking at chamber volumes (like ejection fraction), it tracks how much the heart muscle itself shortens during systole — and it can catch failing contraction before EF ever budges.

1
What "strain" actually measures

Strain is the percentage change in length of a myocardial segment during the cardiac cycle. Longitudinal strain measures shortening along the long axis of the ventricle, from base to apex. GLS is measured using speckle-tracking echocardiography: the software follows the natural acoustic "speckle" pattern of the myocardium frame-by-frame and computes how far each segment moves.

Because the muscle shortens, strain values are negative. Normal GLS is roughly −18% to −20% (or more negative). A less negative value (e.g. −12%) means worse function — a common exam trap, since −12% is a bigger number than −20% but represents poorer contraction.

2
Why GLS beats the eyeball EF

The longitudinal (subendocardial) fibres are the most vulnerable in the myocardium and are the first to fail in almost every disease process. GLS interrogates precisely these fibres, so it flags subclinical / early systolic dysfunction while the ejection fraction — dominated by the more robust circumferential and radial function — remains normal.

Longitudinal fibres fail first→GLS drops early while EF is still "normal"

GLS is also angle-independent, more reproducible and less load-dependent than a visually estimated EF. Its main weakness is that absolute values are vendor-dependent, so serial scans should ideally use the same machine and software.

Averaged from the three standard apical views (4-chamber, 2-chamber, 3-chamber) into a single global value.
Displayed as a colour-coded "bull's-eye" polar map so regional strain can be read segment by segment.
A relative fall >15% from a patient's own baseline is the threshold that matters, not a single absolute reading.
3
Where GLS is used clinically
💊
Cardio-oncology
Serial GLS during cardiotoxic chemo (anthracyclines, trastuzumab). A relative fall >15% predicts later cardiotoxicity and triggers cardioprotection before EF falls.
🍒
Amyloidosis
Classic apical sparing ("cherry on top") bull's-eye pattern — reduced basal/mid strain with preserved apex.
📈
Early disease
Detects subclinical dysfunction in hypertensive heart disease, diabetes, aortic stenosis and HFpEF before EF drops.
🔮
Prognosis
A more powerful predictor of outcome than EF across many conditions, including heart failure and valvular disease.
🚩 A significant serial drop in GLS (relative fall >15% from baseline) in a patient on cardiotoxic chemotherapy signals subclinical cancer-therapy-related cardiac dysfunction (CTRCD). Refer to cardio-oncology for cardioprotection even if the ejection fraction is still normal — waiting for EF to fall means waiting for established, less reversible damage.
🎓 Remember the sign convention: strain is negative because muscle shortens, so "more negative = better". −20% is healthy; −12% is sick. GLS fails early because it reads the vulnerable subendocardial longitudinal fibres — making it the perfect early-warning tool when EF is still reassuringly normal.

Ultrasound is the first-line investigation for a palpable thyroid nodule or goitre. A high-frequency linear probe assesses gland size, echotexture and any focal nodules, then reports each nodule with a risk-stratification score (in the UK, the BTA U-classification U1–U5; internationally, TI-RADS). Crucially, ultrasound assesses structure — thyroid function is a blood test (TFTs), and a "hot" toxic nodule is a radionuclide-uptake concept, not an ultrasound one.

1Why ultrasound first

US is cheap, radiation-free and superb at soft-tissue characterisation. It confirms whether a lump is thyroid or extra-thyroid, distinguishes solid from cystic, measures the gland, screens the cervical nodal chains, and guides fine-needle aspiration (FNA). It also assesses retrosternal extension — though a large or retrosternal goitre is better delineated with CT.

Palpable thyroid nodule / goitre→High-resolution neck ultrasound first, plus TFTs
2Suspicious versus benign features

The report hinges on a handful of malignant sonographic features. Learn the suspicious cluster and the reassuring counterparts.

🔎Solid & hypoechoic
Darker than surrounding parenchyma and non-cystic — the core suspicious combination.
✨Microcalcifications
Punctate bright foci (psammoma bodies) — strongly associated with papillary carcinoma.
📐Taller-than-wide
AP dimension > transverse — growth against tissue planes suggests malignancy.
🌵Irregular margins
Lobulated, spiculated or ill-defined edge; increased intranodular vascularity adds concern.
🫧Abnormal nodes
Rounded, hyperechoic or cystic cervical nodes with microcalcification imply nodal spread.
☄️Benign signs
Purely cystic/spongiform, colloid with "comet-tail" artefact, isoechoic, well-defined halo.
Solid + hypoechoic + microcalcifications + taller-than-wide is the classic quartet for papillary thyroid cancer.
Comet-tail artefact behind a bright colloid focus is a reassuring, near-pathognomonic benign sign.
3U-scoring and what triggers FNA

The BTA U-classification stratifies nodules: U1 normal, U2 benign, U3 indeterminate/equivocal, U4 suspicious, U5 malignant. Nodules scored U3–U5 warrant ultrasound-guided FNA cytology, reported with the Thy classification (Thy1–Thy5). US-guided FNA is the pivotal next step for any indeterminate or suspicious nodule — it converts an imaging suspicion into a tissue diagnosis and directs the MDT.

Nodule scored U3, U4 or U5→Ultrasound-guided FNA → Thy cytology → thyroid MDT
4Diffuse thyroid disease

Beyond focal nodules, US patterns the whole gland. Graves' disease: diffusely enlarged, hypervascular gland — the exuberant colour-Doppler signal is nicknamed the "thyroid inferno." Hashimoto's thyroiditis: heterogeneous, hypoechoic, coarse/micronodular texture, often with fibrous septa. Correlate always with TFTs and autoantibodies — the ultrasound describes the gland, the bloods define its function.

"Thyroid inferno" on colour Doppler = florid vascularity of Graves' disease.
Micronodular, hypoechoic gland with autoantibodies = Hashimoto's.
🚩 A solid hypoechoic nodule with microcalcifications, taller-than-wide shape and abnormal cervical nodes (U4/U5) suggests thyroid cancer — arrange urgent US-guided FNA and thyroid MDT referral. A rapidly enlarging, hard fixed neck mass with hoarseness or stridor (recurrent laryngeal nerve involvement / airway compromise) suggests anaplastic carcinoma or thyroid lymphoma — treat as an emergency and refer urgently.
🎓 Ultrasound tells you what a thyroid lump looks like, not what it does. If a nodule is toxic on bloods, you go to radionuclide scanning; if it is U3–U5 on ultrasound, you go to FNA. Never let a normal TSH reassure you out of characterising a suspicious-looking nodule.

Ultrasound is the first-line tool for characterising a neck lump or cervical lymphadenopathy, for staging head & neck and thyroid cancer, and for guiding FNA or core biopsy. The core skill is separating a benign reactive node from a suspicious (malignant) one using shape, the fatty hilum, cortex and vascular pattern — then acting on red-flag features.

1Find the node and describe it systematically

Scan the neck by level (I–VI) so you can report location reproducibly. For every abnormal node record: size (short-axis is most useful), number, shape, presence of an echogenic fatty hilum, cortical appearance, and vascular pattern on Doppler. These features — not size alone — drive the benign-versus-suspicious call.

2Recognise the benign (reactive) node

A reassuring reactive node is oval, with a long-to-short axis ratio >2, a preserved central echogenic fatty hilum, a smooth thin cortex, and hilar vascularity (vessels entering centrally from the hilum) on colour Doppler.

Oval + fatty hilum + central hilar flow → benign reactive node — reassure, consider interval follow-up
Ratio >2 (longer than it is wide) favours benign.
A crisp fatty hilum is the single most reassuring sign.
3Recognise the suspicious (malignant) node

Malignant and metastatic nodes turn round (short axis increases, ratio <2) and lose the fatty hilum. Look for cortical thickening or eccentric cortex, peripheral / chaotic capsular vascularity, cystic or necrotic change (classic in papillary thyroid and in squamous cell / HPV-related oropharyngeal metastasis), microcalcification (papillary thyroid mets), and matting of adjacent nodes.

⬤Round shape
Short axis increased, L:S ratio <2.
✖Lost hilum
Absent echogenic fatty hilum; thickened/eccentric cortex.
◉Peripheral flow
Chaotic capsular vascularity, not central hilar.
◐Cystic / calcified
Necrosis (SCC/papillary) or microcalcification (papillary mets).
4Special patterns: TB and lymphoma

Tuberculous nodes are typically matted and necrotic, and may form a cold abscess or discharging sinus. Lymphomatous nodes are often multiple, rounded and strikingly hypoechoic (“pseudocystic”) with a reticular internal pattern — but a hilar-type vascularity may persist, which can mislead you toward “benign.” FNA is often insufficient to subtype lymphoma, so a core or excision biopsy is needed.

Multiple rounded hypoechoic “pseudocystic” nodes + B-symptoms → suspect lymphoma — arrange core / excision biopsy
5Sample and stage

For any suspicious node, perform US-guided FNA (or core biopsy) and document node level, size and number to support staging of head & neck or thyroid primaries. Ultrasound also guides which node to target — sample the most abnormal, not simply the largest.

🚩 A hard, fixed, painless, enlarging cervical node in an adult — especially aged >45, a smoker or heavy drinker, or with hoarseness, dysphagia or otalgia — is head & neck squamous cell carcinoma until proven otherwise. Make a 2-week-wait ENT referral for US-guided FNA/core and panendoscopy. Persistent unexplained lymphadenopathy with B-symptoms should prompt core biopsy for lymphoma.
🎓 The fatty hilum is your anchor: an oval node with a preserved central hilum and hilar flow is almost always reactive, whereas a round node that has lost its hilum with peripheral flow, cystic/necrotic change or microcalcification is suspicious — and remember lymphoma can keep a hilar vascular pattern, so never let “central flow” alone reassure you when the clinical picture is worrying.

Scrotal ultrasound with colour Doppler is the first-line imaging for scrotal pain, swelling and palpable masses. It answers three questions fast: is there flow? (torsion vs epididymo-orchitis), is the mass inside or outside the testis? (solid intratesticular = cancer until proven otherwise), and is the tunica intact? (trauma). The single non-negotiable rule: a classic torsion story goes to theatre, not to the scanner.

1Torsion — a clinical diagnosis and surgical emergency

Sudden severe unilateral testicular pain, often with nausea and a high-riding transverse testis. Do not delay exploration for imaging if the story is classic — the window to save the testis is roughly 6 hours. When ultrasound is performed it shows reduced or absent intratesticular colour Doppler flow, an enlarged hypoechoic (oedematous) testis, and the "whirlpool sign" of the twisted spermatic cord. Management is immediate scrotal exploration, detorsion and bilateral orchidopexy (fixation), because the contralateral testis shares the bell-clapper anomaly.

Acute severe pain + absent intratesticular Doppler flow→Torsion — theatre now, bilateral fixation
2Flow tells torsion from epididymo-orchitis

Epididymo-orchitis is the main clinical mimic of torsion but has the opposite Doppler picture: an enlarged, hyperaemic epididymis and/or testis with increased colour flow, often a reactive hydrocele. It usually has a more gradual onset with dysuria or urethral symptoms. Colour Doppler is therefore the decisive discriminator — increased flow points to infection, decreased/absent flow to torsion.

Torsion: reduced/absent flow, enlarged hypoechoic testis, whirlpool cord.
Epididymo-orchitis: increased flow, hyperaemic epididymis/testis, reactive hydrocele.
3Any solid intratesticular mass = cancer until proven otherwise

A solid mass within the testis is a germ cell tumour (seminoma or non-seminomatous) until proven otherwise. Pathway: urgent urology referral, tumour markers AFP, β-hCG and LDH, staging CT, and radical inguinal orchidectomy. Never perform a trans-scrotal biopsy — it seeds tumour and disrupts lymphatic drainage. Contrast this with extratesticular lesions, which are almost always benign.

4Extratesticular benign lesions and trauma
💧Hydrocele
Anechoic fluid surrounding the testis; transilluminates clinically.
🪱Varicocele
"Bag of worms" pampiniform veins >2–3 mm, augment on Valsalva, usually left.
🫧Epididymal cyst / spermatocele
Well-defined anechoic extratesticular cyst; benign, common.
⚪Microlithiasis
Multiple tiny echogenic foci; monitored, associated with GCT risk.
💥Testicular rupture
Breach of tunica albuginea after trauma; heterogeneous testis — needs surgery.
New right-sided or non-reducing varicocele→Image the retroperitoneum/kidney for an obstructing mass
🚩 Acute severe testicular pain with absent intratesticular Doppler flow = torsion: go straight to surgical exploration and bilateral fixation — do not wait for imaging. A solid intratesticular mass = cancer until proven otherwise: urgent urology, tumour markers, radical inguinal orchidectomy — never a scrotal biopsy.
🎓 Doppler flow is the pivot of the acute scrotum: absent flow screams torsion (theatre, not scanner), increased flow points to epididymo-orchitis. For masses, location decides fear — inside the testis and solid means cancer, outside means almost always benign.

Breast ultrasound is a core part of the triple assessment of a breast lump — clinical examination + imaging + biopsy. It is the first-line imaging in women under ~40 (whose denser breasts limit mammography) and complements mammography in older women. It also guides needle biopsy and evaluates the axillary lymph nodes.

1Where US fits in triple assessment
Triple assessment is the gold-standard workup of any breast lump: clinical examination, imaging (US and/or mammography), and tissue biopsy. US is preferred in younger women (<~40) because dense fibroglandular tissue makes mammograms hard to read, and it involves no ionising radiation. In older women it is used alongside mammography to characterise a focal abnormality. US also targets and guides biopsy and assesses the axilla for nodal disease.
Woman <40 with a palpable lump→Ultrasound first-line, not mammography
2Reading benign features
Reassuring sonographic features cluster together: oval shape, wider-than-tall (long axis parallel to skin), well-circumscribed with a smooth thin capsule, hypo- or isoechoic, and few internal echoes.
Fibroadenoma — young women; mobile, firm, oval, gently lobulated, homogeneous and hypoechoic.
Simple cyst — anechoic (black), thin smooth wall, posterior acoustic enhancement; can be aspirated if symptomatic.
3Reading suspicious features
Malignant features are the mirror image of benign ones:
📐Taller-than-wide
Non-parallel, vertical growth crossing tissue planes.
✳️Irregular margins
Spiculated or angular, poorly defined edges.
🌑Posterior shadowing
Dark shadow behind a hypoechoic mass.
⚪Microcalcification
Internal bright specks; ductal extension, distortion.
🫘Abnormal nodes
Cortical thickening, loss of fatty hilum in axilla.
Findings are reported with a scoring system — U1–U5 (or BI-RADS), where U1 is normal and U5 is highly suspicious of malignancy.
4From image to tissue, plus other uses
Any suspicious lesion proceeds to US-guided core biopsy for histology (± FNA of abnormal nodes for cytology). US real-time guidance ensures the needle samples the target accurately. Beyond lumps, US evaluates a breast abscess — a complex collection in lactational mastitis, managed by aspiration or drainage — and assesses implant integrity.
U4/U5 lesion or abnormal node→US-guided core biopsy ± FNA for tissue diagnosis
🚩 An irregular, taller-than-wide, hypoechoic mass with posterior shadowing and abnormal axillary nodes is breast cancer until proven otherwise — refer to the 2-week-wait breast clinic for triple assessment and core biopsy. A persistent solid lump needs tissue diagnosis even if imaging looks benign.
🎓 Benign vs malignant on US is largely about orientation and margins: benign lesions lie flat and smooth (oval, wider-than-tall, circumscribed), malignant ones grow up and out (taller-than-wide, spiculated, shadowing). But imaging never overrules a persistent lump — when clinical suspicion and imaging disagree, biopsy wins.

Ultrasound is the first-line imaging test for a salivary gland swelling. It is cheap, radiation-free, guides needle biopsy, and readily distinguishes the common culprits: stones, inflammation, and tumours. The three glands assessed are the parotid, submandibular, and sublingual.

1Scan the glands systematically
A normal gland is homogeneous and mildly hyperechoic relative to adjacent muscle, with smooth margins. Compare side-to-side. Trace the duct (Wharton's duct for the submandibular, Stensen's duct for the parotid) looking for dilatation. Add colour Doppler to assess vascularity, and interrogate the cervical nodal chains. Remember the deep lobe of the parotid and the facial nerve are poorly seen on US — MRI is superior there.
2Sialolithiasis — the salivary stone
The commonest cause of obstruction, and around 80% occur in the submandibular gland (Wharton's duct) because its secretions are mucinous and it drains uphill. Classic presentation is mealtime pain and swelling that settles between meals. On US the stone is a bright echogenic focus with posterior acoustic shadowing, frequently with proximal ductal dilatation behind the obstruction.
Echogenic focus + posterior shadowing + dilated duct→sialolithiasis
3Sialadenitis — the inflamed gland
A diffusely enlarged, hypoechoic, hypervascular gland. Causes include acute bacterial infection, viral (e.g. mumps parotitis), and obstruction from a stone. Look for a complex, thick-walled fluid collection which indicates an abscess. The cp-reads below summarise the pattern.
Diffuse enlargement
Hypoechoic parenchyma
Increased Doppler flow (hypervascular)
Complex collection = abscess
4Tumours — mostly benign in the parotid
The majority of parotid tumours are benign. US characterises a focal mass and guides FNA or core biopsy.
🟢Pleomorphic adenoma
Commonest salivary tumour. Well-defined, lobulated, hypoechoic mass, usually in the superficial lobe of the parotid.
🔵Warthin's tumour
Cystic, often bilateral. Classically in older male smokers. Benign.
🔴Malignant features
Ill-defined/infiltrative irregular margins, abnormal cervical nodes, and facial nerve involvement.
5Sjögren's syndrome — the leopard-skin gland
Autoimmune destruction produces multiple small hypo-/anechoic areas throughout the gland, giving a heterogeneous "leopard-skin" or honeycomb appearance. Bilateral involvement is typical, and there is an important long-term lymphoma risk, so new focal masses in a Sjögren's gland warrant scrutiny.
Bilateral heterogeneous honeycomb glands→Sjögren's syndrome
🚩 A salivary mass with pain, rapid growth, fixation to surrounding tissue, or facial nerve palsy suggests malignancy. Facial nerve palsy with a parotid mass is malignant until proven otherwise — arrange urgent head & neck/ENT referral, US-guided biopsy, and MRI.
🎓 US answers the first question (stone vs inflammation vs tumour) and guides the needle, but it does not stage. For a suspected malignancy, or to assess the deep parotid lobe and facial nerve, MRI is the definitive next step.

A patient presents with a palpable lump under the skin. Before anyone reaches for a scalpel, the question is simple: is this a boring benign lump you can reassure, or something that needs the sarcoma pathway? Ultrasound is the first-line test that triages exactly this — cheap, quick, dynamic, and able to characterise most superficial soft-tissue masses.

1Why ultrasound first?

A palpable subcutaneous or soft-tissue lump is the bread-and-butter of primary care and surgical clinics. Ultrasound is the first-line imaging modality: no ionising radiation, real-time assessment of compressibility and mobility, and colour Doppler to interrogate vascularity. Its job is to sort lumps into three buckets — obviously benign (reassure, no follow-up), indeterminate, or suspicious (red-flag features → onward pathway).

Classic lipoma or cyst on US→reassure, discharge, no follow-up needed
Indeterminate or red-flag features→MRI + sarcoma MDT + image-guided core biopsy
2The benign line-up: pattern recognition

Most superficial lumps fall into a handful of stereotyped US appearances. Learn these and you have covered the vast majority of clinic referrals.

Lipoma — well-defined, soft and compressible, elongated and lying parallel to the skin, iso- to hyperechoic relative to surrounding fat, with thin internal echogenic striations and minimal or no vascularity. Classic appearances need no follow-up.
Sebaceous / epidermoid cyst — well-defined, sitting within the skin/subcutis, often with a visible punctum; hypoechoic with internal debris and posterior acoustic enhancement.
Ganglion — anechoic, well-defined cyst adjacent to a joint or tendon sheath, classically at the dorsal wrist; may show a neck tracking to the joint.
Abscess — complex collection with internal debris, an avascular centre (no internal Doppler flow) but a hyperaemic surrounding rim; may be aspirated or drained.
Vascular lesion (haemangioma / AVM) — colour Doppler demonstrates internal flow, the key discriminator.
Lymph node — reniform shape with a preserved echogenic fatty hilum and hilar vascularity.
Foreign body / granuloma — echogenic focus (e.g. wood, glass) often with posterior shadowing and a surrounding hypoechoic granulomatous reaction.
3The features that must not be missed

A soft-tissue sarcoma can masquerade as an innocent lump. The following clinical and sonographic red flags flip the diagnosis to sarcoma until proven otherwise.

📏Large — >5 cm
Size over 5 cm is one of the strongest single predictors of malignancy.
⬇️Deep to fascia
A mass extending deep to the deep fascia is far more concerning than a superficial one.
🪨Hard & fixed
A firm, non-compressible, immobile lump is not a lipoma.
📈Rapidly enlarging
A lump that is growing quickly, painful, or recurs after previous excision.
🌫️Heterogeneous
Irregular margins and a mixed, non-uniform internal echotexture.
🩸Internal vascularity
Disorganised internal colour Doppler flow within a solid mass.
Any red flag present→refer to sarcoma centre — do NOT simply excise
🚩 A lump that is >5 cm, deep to fascia, hard, or rapidly growing is a soft-tissue sarcoma until proven otherwise. Refer to a specialist sarcoma centre for MRI and image-guided core biopsy BEFORE any excision. An unplanned "whoops" excision contaminates tissue planes, forces wider re-excision, and worsens long-term outcomes.
🎓 Ultrasound is a triage tool, not the final word. A classic lipoma or cyst can be confidently reassured and discharged, but anything indeterminate — and every red-flag lump — belongs on the MRI + sarcoma MDT pathway with a planned core biopsy. When in doubt, image and refer before you cut.
ULTRASOUND__MSK:
Ultrasound is the first-line, dynamic imaging test for suspected rotator cuff pathology and subacromial impingement. It lets you scan the tendons while the patient moves, is cheap, uses no radiation, allows direct side-to-side comparison, and can guide a targeted injection in the same sitting.

1Know the cuff you are scanning
The rotator cuff is four tendons: supraspinatus (by far the most commonly injured), infraspinatus, teres minor and subscapularis. A normal tendon is a uniform, fibrillar, moderately echogenic band that hugs the humeral head. The long head of biceps tendon and the subacromial-subdeltoid bursa are checked in the same protocol.
2Full-thickness vs partial-thickness tear
A full-thickness tear is a defect spanning the entire tendon: non-visualisation or retraction of the tendon, fluid tracking through the gap, and a bare or "naked" greater tuberosity with the deltoid falling directly onto the cartilage. A partial-thickness tear is a focal hypoechoic/anechoic defect on the bursal or articular surface that does not cross the full width of the tendon.
Deltoid sags onto a bare greater tuberosity + fluid in the gap→full-thickness cuff tear
3Read the other cuff pathologies
Tendinopathy — a thickened, heterogeneous, hypoechoic tendon with loss of the normal fibrillar pattern but no discrete tear.
Calcific tendinitis — a bright echogenic calcific deposit, often with posterior acoustic shadowing, within supraspinatus; acutely it is intensely painful.
Subacromial-subdeltoid bursitis — a distended, fluid-filled or thickened bursa (>2 mm) superficial to the cuff.
Biceps long head tendon — fluid in the sheath, subluxation out of the groove, or frank tear.
🩻Full-thickness tear
Defect through whole tendon, retraction, fluid in gap, naked greater tuberosity.
🔦Calcific deposit
Echogenic focus ± acoustic shadow in supraspinatus; very painful acutely.
💧Bursitis
Distended fluid-filled or thickened subacromial-subdeltoid bursa.
🏃Dynamic impingement
Bunching of cuff/bursa under the acromion on active abduction.
4When to reach for MRI
Ultrasound is operator-dependent and cannot see deep to bone. MRI is used for surgical planning, deep or large/massive tears, muscle atrophy and fatty infiltration, and labral or bony detail that ultrasound cannot resolve.
🚩 An acute large full-thickness cuff tear in a younger patient after significant trauma — with true weakness and a positive drop-arm test — warrants prompt orthopaedic/surgical referral to consider early repair, before the tendon retracts and the muscle degenerates.
🎓 Watch the mimics: a globally stiff, passively restricted shoulder with a normal-looking cuff is more likely adhesive capsulitis (frozen shoulder) than a tear, and always consider referred pain (cervical spine, cardiac, diaphragmatic). Ultrasound answers the cuff question — the clinical picture decides whether the cuff is even the problem.

Musculoskeletal ultrasound is a dynamic, high-resolution, radiation-free tool for imaging tendons and soft tissue. It scans in real time, compares side-to-side, and images through movement — but it is highly operator-dependent, and one artefact (anisotropy) trips up the unwary at every list.

1The normal tendon & the anisotropy trap

On long axis a normal tendon shows an ordered fibrillar echotexture — tightly packed parallel bright (hyperechoic) lines running along the tendon. On short axis it looks like a stippled bright oval. This ordered pattern is your reference for normality.

Probe not perpendicular to the tendon→tendon falsely appears dark (hypoechoic) — ANISOTROPY, an artefact, NOT pathology

Anisotropy vanishes when you angle the probe ("toggle" / "heel-toe") to make the beam strike the fibres at 90°; real tendinopathy stays hypoechoic whatever the angle. This is the classic pitfall — never call a tear or tendinopathy on a single non-perpendicular image.

2Tendinopathy

Chronic overuse (degenerative, not truly "inflammatory") gives a tendon that is thickened, hypoechoic, with loss of the fibrillar pattern. Colour/power Doppler shows neovascularity — abnormal blood flow within the substance of the tendon, correlating with pain.

Achilles tendinopathy — mid-portion fusiform swelling
Patellar tendinopathy — "jumper's knee", proximal deep fibres
Common extensor origin — lateral epicondyle = tennis elbow
Common flexor origin — medial epicondyle = golfer's elbow
3Tendon tears — partial vs complete

A partial tear shows focal fibre discontinuity — a hypoechoic/anechoic cleft interrupting some, but not all, of the fibrillar bundle. A full-thickness / complete tear shows discontinuity across the whole tendon with a gap, retraction of the ends, and refractile (bright) torn edges; the gap may fill with haematoma.

Gentle dynamic movement of the joint under the probe→tendon ends separate / do not move together = confirms a COMPLETE tear

Achilles rupture is the classic: a gap with retracted ends and a positive dynamic test on ultrasound; clinically the calf-squeeze (Simmonds / Thompson) test fails to plantarflex the foot. Ultrasound helps quantify the gap and guide management.

4Sheath & insertion: tenosynovitis and enthesitis

Tenosynovitis = fluid and/or thickening within the tendon sheath, often with hyperaemia on Doppler; the tendon core may be normal. Classic example: De Quervain's tenosynovitis of the first extensor compartment (abductor pollicis longus / extensor pollicis brevis) at the radial wrist.

Enthesitis = inflammation at the bony insertion (enthesis) — hypoechoic thickening, cortical irregularity, sometimes erosions or enthesophytes and Doppler signal — a hallmark of spondyloarthropathy.

5Other soft-tissue targets & guided procedures
💪Muscle tear / haematoma
Fibre disruption with a hypo/anechoic collection; graded and followed for re-bleed or myositis ossificans.
💧Bursitis
Distended, fluid-filled bursa ± wall thickening and Doppler (e.g. subacromial, trochanteric).
🫧Ganglion cyst
Well-defined anechoic cyst with posterior enhancement, no internal flow; common at the wrist.
📌Foreign body
Echogenic focus (wood, glass) ± posterior acoustic shadow and surrounding hypoechoic halo/oedema.
🦶Morton's neuroma
Hypoechoic mass in the intermetatarsal space; painful on sonographic Mulder's manoeuvre.
🎯Image-guided intervention
Real-time needle guidance for joint/bursa aspiration and steroid or PRP injection.
🚩 A complete tendon rupture (e.g. Achilles) needs prompt orthopaedic referral for splinting/immobilisation versus surgical repair — do not discharge. Separately, a hot, swollen, tender joint or tendon with fever raises septic arthritis / infective tenosynovitis: this is an emergency requiring urgent aspiration (Gram stain, culture) and empirical antibiotics — do not inject steroid into a possibly infected structure.
🎓 Before you diagnose any dark tendon, angle the probe: if the hypoechogenicity disappears it was anisotropy (artefact); if it persists, is thickened and shows neovascularity, it is real tendinopathy. Anisotropy is the single most common reason a normal tendon gets called abnormal — and a normal-looking one gets called torn.

A swollen joint is a diagnostic fork: is there fluid inside, and if so, what kind? Ultrasound answers both — it is more sensitive than palpation or plain film for detecting an effusion, is radiation-free, and lets you put a needle exactly where the fluid is. Your job at the probe is to detect fluid, characterise it (simple vs complex, effusion vs synovitis vs crystal), and guide a safe aspiration when it matters.

1Detect the effusion

Scan the joint's dependent recess (suprapatellar pouch at the knee, anterior recess at the hip, dorsal recess at small joints). Fluid distends the capsule and appears as an abnormal collection displacing the normal capsular fat. US picks up effusions far too small to feel or to see on plain film, which is why it outperforms clinical exam.

Anechoic collection distends the recess and squashes when you press→effusion present, and it is a simple fluid
2Simple vs complex fluid

A simple effusion is anechoic (uniformly black), and is compressible / displaceable — press with the probe and the fluid shifts. This is the reassuring transudate/simple pattern (e.g. osteoarthritis, reactive).

A complex effusion contains internal echoes, debris, floating particles or septations. Echoes inside the fluid mean cells or protein: this raises haemarthrosis (blood — trauma, anticoagulation), pus (septic arthritis) or inflammatory debris. Complexity does not tell you the exact fluid — but it tells you to aspirate.

Anechoic + compressible = simple effusion, low-worry pattern.
Internal echoes / septations / debris = complex effusion — think blood, pus or inflammatory sludge, and get fluid.
3Effusion vs synovitis

The classic trap: thickened synovium can mimic fluid. Distinguish them with two moves — compression and Doppler.

💧Effusion
Anechoic, compressible and displaceable, no Doppler flow inside it.
🔥Synovitis
Hypoechoic thickened synovium, non-compressible, with increased power Doppler flow — a marker of active inflammation (rheumatoid / inflammatory arthritis).
Non-compressible hypoechoic tissue lighting up on power Doppler→active synovitis, not simple fluid — flags inflammatory disease activity
4Crystal clues

US can suggest crystal disease before the fluid is even aspirated:

Gout (urate): the double contour sign — a hyperechoic line of urate deposited on top of the cartilage surface, running parallel to the bright bony cortex; plus tophi and hyperechoic aggregates.
Pseudogout (CPPD): hyperechoic deposits within the substance of the cartilage itself (chondrocalcinosis) — inside the cartilage, not on its surface.
5Guide the aspiration

US-guided arthrocentesis improves accuracy and safety — you place the needle tip in the fluid under direct vision, avoid vessels and nerves, and confirm you have actually entered the collection. This is especially valuable for deep joints like the hip, where landmarks are unreliable. The same guidance is used for therapeutic injection.

Deep or difficult joint with an effusion needing sampling→US-guided aspiration for a first-pass, safe diagnostic tap
🚩 A hot, swollen, painful joint is SEPTIC ARTHRITIS until proven otherwise. This is a joint-destroying emergency. Perform urgent aspiration (US-guided or landmark) and send fluid for urgent Gram stain, culture, WCC and crystals BEFORE starting antibiotics. Management is prompt washout and IV antibiotics — do not delay for imaging niceties. In a child with hip pain, US detects an effusion and helps separate transient synovitis from a septic hip: if septic arthritis is suspected, aspirate.
🎓 Two probe manoeuvres crack most swollen joints: compress (fluid moves, synovium doesn't) and add Doppler (synovitis lights up, effusion stays dark). But never let ultrasound characterisation talk you out of tapping a hot joint — echoes cannot exclude pus, and only fluid analysis rules out sepsis.
