Ultrasound-guided injection uses real-time imaging to place a needle precisely into a target compartment — a joint, bursa, tendon sheath or ganglion — or to aspirate fluid accurately. Because you watch the needle tip advance and confirm the target on screen, US-guided injections are consistently more accurate than blind/landmark injections, which matters most for deep or small targets.

1Why image-guide at all?
Blind (landmark) injections rely on surface anatomy and feel, and studies repeatedly show mis-placement — steroid ends up in the wrong compartment or even intratendinous. US lets you see the needle, see the target, and see the injectate spread. Advantages over blind and over fluoroscopy: superior accuracy, real-time avoidance of vessels and nerves, direct confirmation of intra-articular/intra-bursal placement, and no ionising radiation.
2In-plane vs out-of-plane
In-plane: the needle runs along the long axis of the probe, so the whole shaft and tip are visible as a continuous bright line — the preferred technique because you always know where the tip is. Out-of-plane: the needle crosses the beam perpendicularly and appears only as a single bright dot — quicker but you can lose the true tip depth. When in doubt, favour in-plane for accuracy.
Bright continuous line following the probe long axis→in-plane approach, whole needle visualised
3Confirm placement by watching the injectate
The therapeutic agent (corticosteroid + local anaesthetic, hyaluronic acid, or PRP) is anechoic and can be watched distributing in real time. Correct placement shows fluid filling the intended compartment — distending a bursa or flowing along a tendon sheath. If you see the tissue balloon or the fluid fail to spread, you may be intratendinous — stop and reposition.
Anechoic fluid distending the subacromial-subdeltoid bursa → correct intra-bursal placement
Injectate pooling within tendon fibres with no spread → intratendinous, reposition immediately
4Common targets
A wide range of musculoskeletal targets are amenable to US guidance:
🩻Bursae & joints
Subacromial-subdeltoid bursa (impingement); glenohumeral, hip and knee joints
🖐️Sheaths & hand
De Quervain's tenosynovitis, trigger finger, ganglia, carpal tunnel
🦶Foot
Plantar fascia, Morton's neuroma
5Cautions & complications
Before injecting: obtain consent, check anticoagulation status, and use strict aseptic technique. Complications include infection, a transient post-injection steroid flare (1-2 days), skin depigmentation and subcutaneous fat atrophy at the site, and tendon rupture if steroid is injected into rather than around a tendon. Avoid injecting into any area of suspected infection.
🚩 NEVER inject corticosteroid into an actively infected joint or soft tissue, or through infected skin. Exclude septic arthritis first — aspirate and send for culture before any steroid goes in. Steroid into an infected joint is disastrous. Likewise avoid intratendinous steroid (rupture risk, classically the Achilles): inject around the tendon, never into it.
🎓 The single question every US-guided injection answers in real time is: is the needle tip exactly where I think it is, and is the drug going where I intend? Watch the anechoic injectate spread to prove intra-bursal or intra-articular placement — if it won't spread, you're in the wrong plane. This live confirmation, plus no radiation, is why US guidance beats both blind and fluoroscopic injection for most soft-tissue targets.

Ultrasound of a groin or abdominal wall hernia is a dynamic test — its whole value lies in scanning in real time while the patient strains, coughs, or stands. It is the go-to first-line imaging for a clinically suspected but non-palpable ("occult") hernia and for characterising an undiagnosed groin lump: radiation-free, cheap, and done at the bedside with the patient participating.

1Anchor your anatomy: find the inferior epigastric vessels

The inferior epigastric vessels are the reference landmark for every groin hernia scan. Use colour Doppler to find them running deep to rectus, and trace them to their origin from the external iliac vessels. An inguinal hernia sac is then classified by its relationship to these vessels; a femoral hernia lies below the inguinal ligament entirely.

Sac lateral to the inferior epigastric vessels, entering the deep ring & canal→INDIRECT inguinal hernia
Sac medial to the vessels, pushing straight through the posterior wall→DIRECT inguinal hernia
Lump below & lateral to the pubic tubercle, medial to the femoral vein→FEMORAL hernia (commoner in women, strangulates readily)
2Make it move: the Valsalva manoeuvre

This is the key strength of ultrasound. Scan over the suspected defect and ask the patient to perform a Valsalva manoeuvre, cough, or stand up. A hernia sac and its contents bulge out through the defect on straining and reduce back on relaxation. This real-time provocation is what reveals an occult hernia that is invisible and impalpable at rest.

Contents that peristalse or contain moving gas = bowel within the sac.
Uniform echogenic, non-peristaltic contents = fat or omentum.
Always record the neck width, reducibility, and Doppler flow within any contained bowel wall.
3Sort the groin lump differential

Not every groin lump is a hernia. Ultrasound reliably distinguishes the classic mimics:

🫘Lymph node
Oval, fatty echogenic hilum, hilar Doppler flow — not connected to the canal.
🩸Saphena varix
Dilated sapheno-femoral junction; collapses on lying flat, fills on standing, colour flow on Doppler.
🟡Lipoma
Soft, compressible echogenic mass, avascular, no neck or reducibility.
🥚Undescended testis
Ovoid structure with mediastinum testis in the canal; check the empty hemiscrotum.
💥Femoral artery aneurysm
Pulsatile anechoic sac with turbulent/yin-yang Doppler flow, continuous with the artery.
💧Cord hydrocele / abscess
Anechoic cystic collection along the cord; an abscess has debris, thick walls, no internal flow.
🚩 An irreducible, tender hernia with overlying skin changes, absent Doppler flow in the contained bowel wall, surrounding free fluid, and dilated obstructed proximal loops signals incarceration / strangulation — a surgical emergency with a real risk of bowel ischaemia and perforation. Do not persist with reduction attempts; make an urgent surgical referral. Femoral hernias have a narrow rigid neck and strangulate far more readily than inguinal ones.
🎓 The single most useful thing ultrasound adds over examination is movement: a lump that bulges out on Valsalva and slides back on relaxation, containing peristalsing bowel or fat crossing a fascial defect, is a hernia — while a saphena varix that vanishes on lying flat, a node with a fatty hilum, or a pulsatile aneurysm are all sorted in seconds by the same probe.

ULTRASOUND__Point-of-Care (POCUS):
FAST (Focused Assessment with Sonography in Trauma) is a rapid bedside point-of-care ultrasound scan used during trauma resuscitation to answer one binary question: is there FREE FLUID? In the trauma context, free fluid is assumed to be blood — haemoperitoneum or haemopericardium. It is fast, repeatable, involves no radiation, and is done at the patient's side without moving them.

1The four standard FAST views
Free fluid collects in dependent recesses and appears as an anechoic (black) stripe. The four core views are: RUQ (hepatorenal recess = Morison's pouch) — the most sensitive/dependent space in a supine patient; LUQ (perisplenic / splenorenal); Pelvis (rectovesical space / pouch of Douglas); and Subxiphoid (subcostal) pericardial view looking for a pericardial effusion or tamponade.
2eFAST — the extended scan
eFAST ("extended") adds bilateral thoracic views. For pneumothorax, look for loss of lung sliding, absent comet-tail artefacts, the "barcode/stratosphere sign" on M-mode, and the lung point (specific for pneumothorax). For haemothorax, look for anechoic fluid collecting above the diaphragm in the thoracic cavity.
Anechoic stripe in Morison's pouch→Free intraperitoneal fluid = blood until proven otherwise
Positive view = black (anechoic) fluid in a dependent recess
M-mode "barcode/stratosphere sign" = no lung sliding = pneumothorax
Lung point = the transition zone; highly specific for pneumothorax
3Interpreting the result
The action depends on haemodynamic status, not the scan alone.
🩸Positive + UNSTABLE
Straight to laparotomy / damage control. Do NOT delay for CT.
🖥️Positive + STABLE
Proceed to CT to characterise and grade the injury.
❓Negative scan
Does NOT exclude injury. If suspicion persists → CT or serial scans/observation.
4Limitations
A negative FAST is insensitive to retroperitoneal bleeds, hollow viscus (bowel) injury, small-volume bleeding, and solid-organ injury without free fluid. FAST is not used to grade solid-organ injury — that is the role of CT.
🚩 An unstable trauma patient with a positive FAST (free intraperitoneal fluid, or pericardial fluid with tamponade) signals life-threatening haemorrhage → immediate surgery / damage control (laparotomy, or pericardial drainage / thoracotomy). Never let scanning delay resuscitation or definitive haemorrhage control.
🎓 Remember: FAST tells you whether to operate, not what the injury is. A positive scan in an unstable patient is a ticket to theatre; a negative scan never rules injury out. Morison's pouch is the first place blood pools in the supine patient — check it first.

Lung ultrasound (LUS) is a point-of-care tool for the breathless, hypoxic or trauma patient. Because aerated lung is full of air, US cannot image lung tissue directly — instead it reads artefacts generated at the pleural line. Learning to distinguish normal (A-line) patterns from pathological (B-line, absent sliding, consolidation, effusion) patterns lets you diagnose pneumothorax, pulmonary oedema, pneumonia and effusion at the bedside in seconds, often faster and more accurately than a supine CXR.

1Normal aerated lung — the reassuring artefacts

Place the probe longitudinally to find the pleural line sitting between two ribs (the "bat sign"). Three findings confirm normal, aerated, apposed pleura:

Lung sliding — shimmering to-and-fro movement of the pleura with each breath, classically described as "ants marching" along the line. Confirms the two pleural layers are apposed and moving.
A-lines — horizontal, hyperechoic reverberation artefacts lying parallel to the pleura at regular repeating intervals. They indicate dry, well-aerated lung.
Seashore sign — on M-mode, still tissue above the pleura gives horizontal "waves" (sky/sea) and the moving lung below gives a granular "sandy beach". Normal = seashore.
Sliding + A-lines + seashore sign→normal aerated lung at that point — pneumothorax and interstitial syndrome effectively excluded here
2Pneumothorax — loss of the normal signs

Air in the pleural space separates the layers, so the visceral pleura no longer moves or generates artefact. LUS is more sensitive than a supine CXR because air collects anteriorly where the probe sits.

Absent lung sliding and absent B-lines/comet tails — the moving artefacts disappear.
Barcode / stratosphere sign — on M-mode the granular "beach" is replaced by uniform horizontal lines all the way down (no movement below the pleura).
Lung point — the exact spot where sliding lung meets non-sliding lung as the patient breathes. This is pathognomonic for pneumothorax and locates its edge.
Absent sliding + barcode sign + a lung point→pneumothorax confirmed

Note: absent sliding alone is not specific — it also occurs in mainstem intubation, pleural adhesions, ARDS and apnoea. The lung point clinches it.

3Interstitial syndrome / pulmonary oedema — B-lines

Fluid or thickening in the interstitium creates B-lines: vertical, hyperechoic "comet-tail" artefacts that arise from the pleura, extend to the bottom of the screen without fading, erase A-lines, and move with lung sliding.

≥3 B-lines in a single field→"wet lung" / interstitial syndrome in that zone

Bilateral, diffuse B-lines suggest cardiogenic pulmonary oedema or ARDS. Focal B-lines can accompany pneumonia or contusion. A few isolated B-lines at the bases can be normal.

4Consolidation and pleural effusion

When lung loses all its air it starts to look like solid tissue, and fluid collections become directly visible.

Consolidation (pneumonia) — "hepatisation": lung takes on a tissue/liver-like echotexture, often with dynamic air bronchograms (branching hyperechoic foci of air that move with respiration).
Pleural effusion — an anechoic (black) collection above the diaphragm. Look for the spine sign (vertebrae visible above the diaphragm because fluid transmits sound), the quad sign, and "jellyfish"/floating collapsed lung within the fluid.

US also guides safe thoracocentesis, marking the largest pocket and avoiding the diaphragm and liver/spleen.

🫧A-lines + sliding
Normal aerated lung — excludes pneumothorax and oedema at that point.
📏Lung point
Pathognomonic for pneumothorax — sliding meets non-sliding lung.
☄️≥3 B-lines
Wet lung — bilateral diffuse suggests cardiogenic oedema or ARDS.
🌊Anechoic + spine sign
Pleural effusion above the diaphragm — guides drainage.
🚩 Tension pneumothorax is a clinical diagnosis, not a radiological one. Absent lung sliding with a barcode sign PLUS haemodynamic compromise, a deviated trachea, distended neck veins or a hyperresonant hemithorax demands immediate needle or finger decompression — do not delay for confirmatory imaging. Likewise, a large effusion causing respiratory distress needs urgent US-guided drainage. Remember absent sliding is not specific on its own (intubation, adhesions, ARDS, apnoea).
🎓 The BLUE protocol ties it together: start at the anterior chest of the breathless patient and read the pleura first. Sliding present + A-lines points away from oedema and pneumothorax; bilateral B-lines point to oedema; absent sliding + lung point confirms pneumothorax; hepatisation or a spine sign at the base points to pneumonia or effusion. Master the four patterns and you can triage a hypoxic patient before the portable X-ray even arrives.

The inferior vena cava (IVC) is a compliant, low-pressure vessel whose calibre reflects right atrial pressure (RAP). At the bedside, a subcostal ultrasound of the IVC becomes a rapid, non-invasive surrogate for volume status and, in context, fluid responsiveness in the shocked or breathless patient — but only ever as one voice in a POCUS chorus, never a solo.

1Getting the view
Place a curvilinear (or phased-array) probe in the subcostal position and obtain a long-axis view of the IVC as it drains into the right atrium. Measure the diameter ~2 cm distal to the hepatic vein/RA junction, perpendicular to the vessel wall. Confirm you are on the IVC (not the aorta) — it is thin-walled, compressible, respirophasic, and joins the RA.
2What to assess
Two things: the maximum IVC diameter and its respiratory variation. In a spontaneously breathing patient, inspiration drops intrathoracic pressure and the IVC collapses — hence collapsibility. In a mechanically ventilated patient the physiology reverses (positive-pressure inspiration distends the IVC), so we speak of distensibility. Collapsibility index = (max − min diameter) / max diameter.
Spontaneous breath in→IVC narrows (negative intrathoracic pressure sucks blood into the chest)
A small IVC (<1–1.5 cm) that collapses >50% suggests low RAP, hypovolaemia, and a patient who is likely fluid-responsive.
A large IVC (>2–2.5 cm) that is plethoric and collapses <50% suggests high RAP / venous congestion — think fluid overload, right heart failure, tamponade, massive PE, tension pneumothorax, or pulmonary hypertension.
3Putting it to work
The IVC helps guide fluid resuscitation in sepsis and undifferentiated shock, distinguish cardiogenic from hypovolaemic shock, assess volume in dialysis and heart-failure patients, and forms a core component of the RUSH and FoCUS shock protocols. Always integrate it with cardiac and lung POCUS and the clinical picture — treat the trend and the patient, not the number.
💧Small & collapsing
<1–1.5 cm, >50% collapse → low RAP, hypovolaemia, likely fluid-responsive. A reasonable cue to give fluid.
🫀Large & plethoric
>2–2.5 cm, <50% collapse → high RAP / venous congestion. Hunt for the obstructive or cardiac cause; do NOT flood with fluid.
⚠️Beware the ventilator
High airway pressures, raised intra-abdominal pressure, isolated RV failure and athletic hearts all confound the reading. It is an adjunct, not a verdict.
🚩 A dilated, non-collapsing IVC with hypotension and a pericardial effusion points to cardiac tamponade (or, with a dilated, strained RV, to massive PE). This is a plethoric, congested IVC — do not give large fluid boluses. Act urgently on the reversible cause (pericardiocentesis, thrombolysis, decompression).
🎓 The IVC is a trend and an adjunct, not a number to treat. A small collapsing IVC nudges you toward fluid; a fat plethoric one warns you off it and sends you looking for tamponade, RV strain, or congestion. Read it alongside cardiac and lung POCUS, and always in the light of the patient in front of you.

A point-of-care bladder scan is a quick bedside ultrasound — either a dedicated automated bladder scanner or a hand-held probe — that estimates bladder volume and post-void residual (PVR) in seconds, without a catheter. It answers one blunt, high-yield ward question: is this deteriorating, oliguric patient in retention (full, tense bladder) or truly anuric (empty bladder)? The answer changes management completely.

1How the volume is calculated

The bladder is modelled as an ellipsoid. Measure three orthogonal diameters in centimetres and apply the ellipsoid formula:

Volume (mL) ≈ height × width × depth × 0.52

Automated scanners fire multiple planes, reconstruct the shape and compute this for you — you simply aim at the suprapubic region and read the number. On a real-time image a full bladder is a smooth anechoic (black) sac with bright posterior acoustic enhancement behind it (sound passes freely through fluid).

2The core ward decision: retention vs anuria

In the patient who has stopped passing urine, do not reach straight for a catheter — scan first.

Empty bladder, still not passing urine→this is not retention — think pre-renal/renal cause or true anuria; a catheter adds infection risk and no benefit
Full, painful, tense bladder (often >600 mL)→acute urinary retention — catheterise and re-scan to confirm decompression
<50 mL residual after voiding = normal complete emptying.
Up to ~100 mL PVR is often acceptable in the elderly.
Persistently raised PVR = incomplete emptying (BPH/outlet obstruction, neurogenic bladder, anticholinergic or opioid drugs).
3Where it earns its keep
🚽Confirm acute retention
Quantify volume before catheterisation, then re-scan after to prove the bladder is empty.
📏Measure PVR
Objective post-void residual to assess emptying and titrate intermittent self-catheterisation.
🛡️Avoid needless catheters
An empty-bladder read spares the patient an unnecessary catheter and its CAUTI risk.
🎯Guide suprapubic catheter
Confirm a distended bladder sits under the puncture site before suprapubic insertion.
4Pitfalls — when the number lies

Automated scanners can over-read when another fluid-filled or complex structure sits in the field: a large ovarian cyst, ascites, or a gravid uterus can all be counted as bladder. If the displayed volume is implausible — a huge number in a patient who has just voided, or a full read with no clinical retention — switch to real-time imaging and look for the true anechoic bladder before acting.

🚩 A grossly distended bladder with bilateral hydronephrosis and a rising creatinine = high-pressure chronic retention causing post-obstructive (obstructive) AKI. Catheterise urgently, monitor renal function, and watch for post-obstructive diuresis with large urine outputs. Acute retention, by contrast, is painful and also needs prompt catheterisation.
🎓 The scanner is a decision tool, not just a number: before every catheter in the anuric or deteriorating patient, ask "full or empty?" An empty bladder redirects you from the outflow tract to the kidneys and the circulation — and saves the patient a catheter they never needed.

Ultrasound-guided vascular access uses real-time imaging to place cannulae into veins (and arteries) under direct vision. NICE recommends 2D ultrasound as the first-line, preferred method for central venous catheter insertion — especially the internal jugular vein — because it raises first-pass success and cuts complications versus the blind landmark technique.

1Identify the vessel — vein vs artery
The single most important skill is telling the target vein apart from its neighbouring artery. Apply gentle probe pressure in the short-axis (transverse) view and watch what happens to each vessel.
Vessel collapses fully with light probe pressure, thin-walled, non-pulsatile, larger, augments (distends) with distal limb compression→VEIN — your target
Round, thick-walled, pulsatile, does NOT compress, smaller→ARTERY — avoid
If in any doubt, use colour or pulsed-wave Doppler: pulsatile high-velocity flow that fills in systole = artery; low-velocity phasic flow = vein.
2Choose your needle approach
Two orientations of probe and needle, each with trade-offs:
◎Short-axis (out-of-plane)
Vessel seen as a circle; needle crosses the beam so only the tip shows as a bright dot. Easy to centre the vessel, but you must fan/walk the probe to keep tracking the true tip.
▬Long-axis (in-plane)
Vessel seen as a tube; the whole needle shaft and tip stay visible in one plane. Best control of depth, but demands steady alignment of needle within the thin scan plane.
3Common uses
Internal jugular, femoral and subclavian/axillary central lines; PICC lines; difficult peripheral IV access; and arterial line insertion (e.g. radial). Ultrasound is especially valued where the anatomy is variable or the vessel is deep.
4Why it beats landmark technique
Compared with the blind landmark method, ultrasound gives higher first-pass success, fewer needle attempts, and fewer complications — reduced inadvertent arterial puncture, less haematoma, and lower pneumothorax risk for IJ/subclavian access.
Confirm the guidewire lies within the vein (not the artery) BEFORE dilating — many operators re-scan the wire in both planes.
Afterwards, check line tip position and exclude pneumothorax with a CXR or lung ultrasound.
🚩 Inadvertent arterial cannulation and dilatation is a serious, potentially fatal complication — signalled by pulsatile bright-red flow and an arterial pressure waveform. If a large-bore catheter has been placed in an artery, do NOT simply pull it out and compress. Leave it in situ and obtain urgent vascular/surgical advice. Always confirm venous placement of the guidewire before dilating.
🎓 The vein compresses, the artery pulsates. If light probe pressure flattens the vessel, it's your target; if it stubbornly stays round and throbs, back off. Confirm the wire is venous before the dilator ever touches skin.

Ultrasound-guided drainage and aspiration uses real-time imaging to sample or drain a fluid collection safely. US identifies a safe window, marks the depth to the target, and keeps the needle away from bowel, vessels and solid organs — either by direct puncture over a marked site or, for catheter placement, by the Seldinger technique (needle → guidewire → dilator → pigtail catheter).

1Why image-guide it at all?
Blind (landmark-only) puncture carries a real risk of hitting the wrong structure. Real-time or marked-site US markedly reduces bleeding, organ injury and pneumothorax. The British Thoracic Society recommends US guidance for pleural procedures — it dramatically cuts the risk of puncturing liver, spleen or lung. US confirms the collection is present, its size, its depth, and that there is a clear window down to it.
Fluid collection needs sampling or draining→US to find a safe window, mark depth, then direct puncture (aspiration) or Seldinger (catheter)
2Direct puncture vs Seldinger
A simple diagnostic aspiration (e.g. a diagnostic pleural or ascitic tap) is a single needle-and-syringe direct puncture. When an indwelling drain is needed, the Seldinger sequence is used: puncture the collection with a needle, thread a soft guidewire through it, remove the needle, pass a dilator over the wire to widen the track, then railroad a pigtail catheter over the wire and remove the wire — the coiled pigtail locks the catheter in place.
Anechoic (black) collection = simple fluid; internal echoes/septations suggest pus, blood or a complex/loculated collection.
Always send fluid for microscopy, culture & sensitivity, biochemistry and cytology as clinically indicated.
Check consent, aseptic technique and coagulation/platelets before puncturing.
3Common procedures you must know
The same principle is applied across the body — the site changes, the logic does not.
🫁Pleural effusion
Diagnostic/therapeutic thoracocentesis and chest-drain insertion. US-guided per BTS to avoid liver/spleen/lung puncture.
🩸Ascitic tap / drain
Diagnostic paracentesis for SBP, or therapeutic large-volume drainage. Classic site left iliac fossa — avoid inferior epigastric vessels.
🦠Abscess drainage
Liver, intra-abdominal or soft-tissue collections drained with catheter placement — source control plus antibiotics.
🩻IR drains
Nephrostomy and biliary drains (interventional radiology), joint aspiration, and pericardiocentesis for tamponade.
🚩 An infected collection under pressure needs urgent drainage as source control alongside antibiotics — think obstructed infected system (pyonephrosis), empyema, or an abscess with sepsis. Likewise, a tense or large collection causing organ compromise — cardiac tamponade or a tension collection — must be drained emergently. Antibiotics alone will not fix an undrained infected pocket.
🎓 US guidance turns a blind, landmark-based stab into a targeted procedure: it proves the fluid is really there, measures the depth, and steers around bowel, vessels and solid organs. If you remember one rule — an infected, obstructed or tense collection is a drainage problem first and an antibiotic problem second.
ULTRASOUND__Paediatric:
Neonatal cranial ultrasound is the first-line neuroimaging of the newborn brain — a cot-side, radiation-free, sedation-free scan performed through the open anterior fontanelle. It is the workhorse of the NICU: it screens preterm infants for haemorrhage and white matter injury, tracks ventricular size over serial scans, and can be repeated as often as clinically needed.

1The acoustic window & why we use it
The anterior fontanelle is a soft, unossified gap in the skull that lets ultrasound waves pass into the brain — bone would otherwise reflect them. It is only usable while the fontanelle remains open (typically closing between ~9 and 18 months), so cranial US is a neonatal/early-infancy tool. Because the probe is brought to the incubator, there is no need to move a sick or ventilated baby, no ionising radiation, and no sedation — ideal for fragile premature neonates.
2Standard indications
The core indication is routine screening of preterm infants — especially those born <32 weeks or <1500 g — for intracranial haemorrhage and white matter injury, usually on a set schedule (e.g. within the first week and again around term-corrected age). Other uses: assessing ventricular size and hydrocephalus, monitoring suspected hypoxic-ischaemic injury, and detecting large congenital malformations or space-occupying lesions.
Preterm <32 weeks / <1500 g→routine screening cranial US for GMH-IVH and PVL
3Germinal matrix / intraventricular haemorrhage (GMH-IVH)
The germinal matrix is a highly vascular, fragile zone near the caudothalamic groove that involutes with maturity — in preterms it bleeds easily, particularly in the first few days of life. Cranial US grades the haemorrhage, which guides prognosis and follow-up:
Grade I — haemorrhage confined to the germinal matrix only.
Grade II — intraventricular haemorrhage without ventricular dilatation.
Grade III — intraventricular haemorrhage with ventricular dilatation.
Grade IV — intraparenchymal haemorrhagic venous infarction (extension into brain tissue).
Serial scans then monitor for post-haemorrhagic ventricular dilatation / hydrocephalus, a common sequela of higher-grade bleeds.
4Periventricular leukomalacia (PVL) & other findings
PVL is the characteristic white matter injury of prematurity: an early periventricular echogenic "flare" evolves over days to weeks into cystic change. It is strongly associated with later cerebral palsy (spastic diplegia). Other recognisable patterns include hypoxic-ischaemic encephalopathy (diffuse cerebral oedema with loss of grey–white differentiation), congenital malformations, and ventriculomegaly.
🩸GMH-IVH
Fragile germinal matrix bleeds; graded I–IV; watch for post-haemorrhagic hydrocephalus.
🧠PVL
Echogenic flare then cysts; linked to spastic diplegic cerebral palsy.
💧Ventriculomegaly
Serial measurement of ventricular size tracks evolving hydrocephalus.
5Limitations — when to reach for MRI
Cranial US is excellent for central, periventricular structures and large lesions but is poor for the posterior fossa (cerebellum, brainstem) and for cortical/peripheral and subtle lesions. MRI is superior for anatomical detail, for prognostication in HIE, and for imaging the posterior fossa — it is the follow-up modality when US is normal but concern persists, or when detailed outcome information is needed.
Normal/equivocal US but ongoing concern, posterior fossa or HIE prognosis needed→MRI brain
🚩 A preterm baby with a sudden drop in haematocrit, apnoea, seizures, a bulging/tense fontanelle or rapidly rising head circumference needs urgent cranial US — this suggests a large IVH or rapidly progressive post-haemorrhagic hydrocephalus. A rapidly enlarging head must be escalated; management may require CSF drainage (e.g. lumbar punctures, reservoir) or a ventriculoperitoneal shunt.
🎓 Think of cranial US as the NICU's "bedside window" — cheap, repeatable and safe, perfect for serial monitoring of the preterm brain, but blind to the posterior fossa and cortex. When the picture is subtle, the head is growing too fast, or you need to prognosticate, the answer is MRI.

Ultrasound is the imaging modality of choice for developmental dysplasia of the hip (DDH) in infants under roughly 4–6 months, because at this age the femoral head is largely cartilaginous and therefore invisible on plain X-ray. US lets you see the cartilaginous head, judge how well the bony acetabulum covers it, and dynamically test stability at the cot-side without ionising radiation.

1Why ultrasound, and why an age window

In a newborn the femoral head has no ossific nucleus yet, so on radiograph it is simply not there — you would be inferring hip position from indirect bony lines. Ultrasound images the cartilage directly, so it is ideal for the young infant. The ossific nucleus typically appears around 4–6 months; once it does, it casts an acoustic shadow that obscures the acetabulum, and plain radiographs take over as the investigation of choice.

Infant < 4–6 months, DDH question→Ultrasound (cartilaginous head)
Infant > 4–6 months / ossific nucleus present→Plain radiograph
2UK screening pathway: NIPE and who gets scanned

Every baby has a Newborn and Infant Physical Examination (NIPE) at birth and again at 6–8 weeks. The hips are tested with two manoeuvres:

Barlow — adduct and gently push posteriorly to see if a located hip can be dislocated (dislocatable hip).
Ortolani — abduct and lift to relocate a dislocated hip back into the acetabulum (a palpable clunk).

A baby with a positive examination OR with risk factors is referred for an ultrasound hip.

3Risk factors that trigger a scan
🍑Breech
Breech presentation, especially at/after 36 weeks or breech at delivery.
🧬Family history
First-degree relative with DDH.
♀️Female / firstborn
Female sex and firstborn raise risk in many pathways.
💧Oligohydramnios
Reduced intrauterine space / oligohydramnios.
4The Graf method: alpha and beta angles

On a standardised coronal view, the Graf method quantifies acetabular development:

Alpha angle — the bony acetabular roof angle. Normal is ≥60°; a lower value means a shallow, dysplastic acetabulum.
Beta angle — the cartilaginous roof angle; rises as the head is less well contained.

Hips are classified type I (normal) through type IV (severe dysplasia/dislocation). A dynamic assessment is added to grade stability — whether the head is subluxable or frankly dislocatable under stress.

5Management

Confirmed DDH in a young infant is treated with a Pavlik harness, which holds the hips flexed and abducted so the head sits deep in the acetabulum and the socket develops normally. Failed harness treatment or later presentation moves to closed or open reduction under anaesthetic, held in a spica cast. Left untreated, DDH causes a limp, leg-length discrepancy, and early osteoarthritis in adulthood.

🚩 A frankly dislocated or irreducible hip, or dysplasia persisting despite harness treatment, needs prompt paediatric orthopaedic referral. Beware the late presenter at walking age — a limp or waddling gait, asymmetric skin creases, and limited hip abduction warrant urgent referral, because reduction becomes far harder the later it is caught.
🎓 Match the imaging to the skeleton, not the calendar alone: the femoral head is cartilage in early infancy, so ultrasound is the tool; once the ossific nucleus appears (~4–6 months) it shadows the acetabulum and the radiograph takes over. Remember Graf’s alpha ≥60° as your marker of a normal bony roof.

A first-born baby boy, six weeks old, is brought in with milk-vomiting that now shoots across the room. He is hungry and ravenous the moment feeding stops — yet the scales say he is losing weight. Ultrasound is the non-invasive investigation of choice that confirms infantile hypertrophic pyloric stenosis (IHPS) without radiation or contrast, letting you image and measure the thickened pylorus in real time.

1Spot the classic clinical picture

Think IHPS in a first-born male, typically 2–8 weeks old, with progressive non-bilious projectile vomiting. The give-away is the behaviour: the baby is hungry and eager to re-feed immediately after vomiting, but is losing weight and becoming dehydrated. On exam you may feel an olive-sized mass in the RUQ/epigastrium and see visible gastric peristalsis crossing the upper abdomen during a test feed.

Non-bilious projectile vomit + still hungry→obstruction proximal to ampulla = pylorus
2Know the classic biochemistry

Persistent vomiting of gastric juice strips out hydrogen and chloride, producing the textbook hypochloraemic hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis. Loss of HCl drives the alkalosis; the kidney then trades potassium to retain hydrogen, deepening the hypokalaemia. This derangement is not a footnote — it governs the entire management sequence.

3Measure the pylorus on ultrasound

The whole diagnosis rests on two measurements of the hypertrophied pyloric muscle:

Pyloric muscle wall thickness ≥ 3 mm — remember the mnemonic "π / 3.14": a wall of roughly 3 mm.
Pyloric channel length ≥ 15–17 mm — the elongated, non-relaxing channel.
Failure of gastric contents to pass through the channel, with a hyperperistaltic stomach churning against the obstruction.
4Recognise the named sonographic signs
🎯Target / doughnut sign
Transverse view: hypoechoic thickened muscle ring encircling the central echogenic mucosa.
📏Cervix sign
Longitudinal view: the elongated pyloric channel indenting the fluid-filled antrum like a cervix.
5Resuscitate first, then operate

IHPS is a medical emergency first, not a surgical rush. Correct the fluid, electrolyte and acid-base derangement with IV fluids, replacing potassium and chloride, until the baby is rehydrated and the alkalosis has resolved. The definitive treatment — Ramstedt pyloromyotomy, splitting the hypertrophied muscle down to (but not through) the mucosa — is performed only once the infant is fully resuscitated.

🚩 Never operate on an unresuscitated baby. Persistent hypokalaemia and metabolic alkalosis markedly raise the risk of post-operative apnoea under anaesthesia. A severely dehydrated, lethargic infant needs urgent fluid resuscitation before theatre — surgery on IHPS is elective in timing, never a rush.
🎓 The behaviour clinches it: any vomiting infant who is still hungry and eager to feed after each projectile vomit should make you reach for the pyloric ultrasound. Wall ≥ 3 mm ("π"), channel ≥ 15–17 mm — measure, correct the alkalosis, then cut.

Intussusception is when one segment of bowel telescopes into the adjacent distal segment (most commonly ileocolic). It is the commonest cause of bowel obstruction in infants, and ultrasound is the first-line and diagnostic imaging test — quick, radiation-free, and highly sensitive.

1Spot the classic clinical picture

Typically an infant or toddler (~3 months–2 years, peak ~6–9 months). The hallmark is intermittent colicky abdominal pain — the child draws up the legs, cries inconsolably in paroxysms, then settles and appears well between episodes. Add vomiting and a palpable sausage-shaped mass, classically in the right upper quadrant.

Episodic crying + drawing up legs + settling in between→Think intussusception until proven otherwise
🚩 "Redcurrant jelly" stool (blood mixed with mucus) is a LATE and ominous sign reflecting bowel ischaemia. Do not wait for it to appear before imaging — its absence does not exclude the diagnosis.
2Read the ultrasound

US is the confirmatory test. The telescoped bowel produces two pathognomonic appearances depending on the plane of imaging.

Transverse: the TARGET / DOUGHNUT sign — concentric alternating hyperechoic and hypoechoic rings of bowel-within-bowel.
Longitudinal: the PSEUDOKIDNEY sign — the layered mass resembles a kidney, with an echogenic centre (compressed mucosa/mesenteric fat) and hypoechoic rim.
3Consider a pathological lead point

Most young infants are idiopathic — hypertrophied lymphoid tissue (Peyer's patches) acting as a lead point, often post-viral (lymphoid hyperplasia). US may identify a discrete pathological lead point, which is more likely in older children and should prompt a search for an underlying cause.

🎯Meckel's diverticulum
Commonest structural lead point in children.
🫧Polyp
Mucosal polyp dragged forward by peristalsis.
🩸Lymphoma
Consider in the older child with a bowel wall mass.
🟣HSP wall haematoma
Henoch-Schönlein purpura causes an intramural bleed acting as a lead point.
4Manage — resuscitate, then reduce

Resuscitate first: IV access with fluid resuscitation and an NG tube for gastric decompression. Once the child is stable and there is no peritonitis or perforation, definitive treatment is air (pneumatic) enema reduction under radiological guidance — the first-line therapeutic option, which is both diagnostic and therapeutic (a contrast enema is the alternative).

Stable, no perforation, no peritonitis→Air enema reduction under radiological guidance

Surgery is indicated if the enema fails, or if there is perforation, peritonitis, shock, or an identified lead point.

🚩 Signs of peritonitis, perforation (free air), or shock are absolute contraindications to enema reduction and mandate urgent surgery. A sick, shocked or peritonitic child needs immediate resuscitation and surgical referral — do not attempt an enema.
🎓 The target/doughnut sign on transverse US and the pseudokidney sign on longitudinal US are the two views to name in an exam. Remember the sequence: ultrasound to diagnose → resuscitate → air enema to treat (if no contraindication) → surgery if it fails or the child is unstable. Redcurrant jelly stool is late, not a screening trigger.
